Endosymbiosis & Food Webs

One story in two parts. Part 1: how eukaryotic cells gained mitochondria and chloroplasts by engulfing bacteria. Part 2: how the organisms built from those cells are connected, through who makes food, who feeds on whom, and the webs that link them.

PART 1

Endosymbiosis

THE QUESTION The mitochondria powering your cells were once free-living bacteria. How do we know?

The short version: a big cell swallowed a small one, kept it, and the two became one. The twelve steps below follow that story in order: what a bacterium is, who was involved, what happened, what it led to, how we can be sure, and what is still unknown.1–5

AN ANIMAL CELL Mitochondria make most of the ATP that powers the cell.
A PLANT CELL Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis. Plant cells have mitochondria too.

Both organelles look oddly like bacteria living inside a bigger cell. That is what they once were.

STEP 1 · BEFORE THE STORY STARTS

A bacterial cell: what it has and what it lacks

The theory is about bacteria that ended up living inside other cells. So start with the bacterium itself. Unlike a eukaryotic cell, a bacterial cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts, and most of its DNA is a single circular chromosome.1,2

Look inside a bacterium

WHAT A BACTERIAL CELL HASSmall and simple, but a complete living thing
A CELL MEMBRANE AND A CELL WALLThe membrane encloses the cell. The wall sits outside it and holds the cell's shape.
ONE CIRCULAR CHROMOSOMEMost of the cell's DNA is a single circular molecule, folded into many loops. It sits loose in the cytoplasm, with nothing around it.
RIBOSOMES IN THE CYTOPLASMThey build the cell's proteins. With no nucleus in the way, they sit right beside the DNA.
SOMETIMESPlasmids: small extra circles of DNA. Flagella: tails that let some bacteria swim.
WHAT A BACTERIAL CELL LACKSNo nucleus, no mitochondria, no chloroplastsThe dashed shapes are the three things a bacterial cell does not have.The DNA is still there, faint in the middle. It simply has no membrane around it, so there is no nucleus.Hold on to this. The whole theory is about how eukaryotic cells came to have two of these three.
WHERE THE ENERGY WORK HAPPENSOn the membrane and in the cytoplasmA bacterium has no mitochondria, yet it still has to get energy out of food. That work is done by proteins floating in the cytoplasm or embedded in the cell membrane.A few bacteria, notably the photosynthetic ones, also have internal membranes, and their light reactions happen there.In a eukaryotic cell the same two jobs happen inside organelles: aerobic respiration in the mitochondrion, photosynthesis in the chloroplast.

A simplified drawing. Prokaryotic cells are small: typically 1 to 2 micrometers across, much smaller than eukaryotic cells.1

WHO HAS WHAT

Three domains of life, side by side

Only one of the three domains has mitochondria and chloroplasts at all. That is the puzzle the rest of this part solves.1

DOMAIN · PROKARYOTES

Bacteria

✕Nucleus
✕Mitochondria
✕Chloroplasts

Divide by binary fission

Energy work: proteins in the cytoplasm and the cell membrane.

DOMAIN · PROKARYOTES

Archaea

✕Nucleus
✕Mitochondria
✕Chloroplasts
One circular chromosome
Divide by binary fission, the same way bacteria do

A separate domain from bacteria. They come back in Step 12.

DOMAIN · EUKARYOTES

Eukaryotes

✓Nucleus
✓Mitochondria: a universal feature. Step 11 covers the rare cells that lost them
✓Chloroplasts, in the photosynthetic ones only
Several linear chromosomes, inside the nucleus
Divide by mitosis and meiosis

Animals, plants, fungi and protists. Energy work happens inside organelles.

THE QUESTION THIS SETS UP Mitochondria are found right across the eukaryotes. No bacterium and no archaeon has them. So where did eukaryotes get them?
That is a bacterial cell. Next: how one becomes two.
STEP 2 · HOW A BACTERIUM MAKES MORE OF ITSELF

Binary fission

When bacterial cells divide, they do it by binary fission: the cell copies its DNA, grows, and splits in two. Eukaryotic cells divide by different processes, mitosis and meiosis.1,2

INTERACTIVE · SIX FRAMES

Watch one cell become two

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
attached to the membraneone circle of DNAcopying starts at one spotand runs both ways roundtwo attachment sitestwo circles of DNAthe sites move apartthe cell gets longerpinches in at the middleabout twice its first sizetwo daughter cellssame DNA in each
1 · BEFORE DIVIDINGOne circular DNA molecule, attached to the membraneThe cell's circular chromosome is held against the inside of the cell membrane by proteins (the pink dot).
2 · COPY THE DNAReplication starts at one spot and runs both waysBinary fission begins with DNA replication. Copying starts at a specific location, the origin of replication, and proceeds in opposite directions around the circle.
3 · TWO CIRCLESEach copy gets its own attachment siteThe result is two DNA molecules, each attached to the membrane at a different site. At first the two sites are close together.
4 · GROWThe cell lengthens and the copies move apartAs the cell elongates, the two attachment sites are carried away from each other, and each takes its DNA circle with it.
5 · PINCHA constriction forms at the midpointWhen the cell is about twice its original size and the two DNA molecules are well separated, the cell pinches in at the middle.
6 · TWO CELLSNew membrane and wall finish the jobNew cell membrane and cell wall are built at the constriction, dividing the one cell into two.Each daughter cell has the same genetic material as the parent cell.
TWO WAYS TO DIVIDE

Bacterial cells and eukaryotic cells do it differently

BACTERIAL CELLSBinary fission. Copy the one circular chromosome, grow, pinch in two.
EUKARYOTIC CELLSMitosis and meiosis. Different processes, built around many linear chromosomes in a nucleus.
HOLD ON TO THESE TWO Circular DNA and binary fission are bacterial signatures. In Step 9 both turn up somewhere surprising: inside your own cells.
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Before moving on

What does binary fission start with?

DNA replication. The circular chromosome is copied first, starting at one spot and running both ways around the circle.

How does each daughter cell end up with its own copy?

Each DNA circle is attached to the cell membrane. As the cell grows longer the two attachment sites move apart, so there is one copy on each side when the cell pinches in two.

Now meet the two bacteria this story is about, and the cell that swallowed them.
STEP 3 · THE CAST

Two free-living bacteria, and the cell that engulfed them

Before any of this happened there were no mitochondria and no chloroplasts anywhere. There were bacteria living on their own, and there was a larger cell that could swallow things. Meet the two bacteria first, as they were: free.1,2

WHAT FREE-LIVING MEANS Not inside any other cell. Each bacterium below is a whole organism: it feeds itself, copies its own DNA and divides by binary fission whenever it is ready. These are not pictures of a mitochondrion and a chloroplast. They are the bacteria those organelles descend from.
THE FIRST BACTERIUM

An alpha-proteobacterium

Bacterium · free-living
FREE-LIVING: no cell around itdividing on its ownoxygen + food in
WHAT IT ISA member of the proteobacteria, the most diverse of all the groups of bacteria. The alpha-proteobacteria are one branch of that group.1,2
HOW IT LIVESOn its own. It takes in small organic molecules and oxygen from its surroundings and gets its energy by aerobic respiration.
INSIDENo nucleus, one circular chromosome. It is a typical bacterial cell, like the one in Step 1.
ITS PART IN THE STORYIts descendants become the mitochondrion.
THE SECOND BACTERIUM

A cyanobacterium

Bacterium · free-living · photosynthetic
FREE-LIVING: no cell around itinternal membranesoxygen outa filament of cells
WHAT IT ISA member of the cyanobacteria, the one group of bacteria that photosynthesizes much as plants and algae do: it uses light and water, and gives off oxygen.1
HOW IT LIVESOn its own, from deserts to the open ocean. Some are single cells, others form balls or filaments.
INSIDENo nucleus, one circular chromosome, and no chloroplast. Its light reactions happen on internal membranes in the cytoplasm.
ITS PART IN THE STORYIts descendants become the chloroplast.
THE HOST

STILL HERE TODAY

Both kinds of bacteria are alive right now

Alpha-proteobacteria and cyanobacteria did not disappear when some of them moved into other cells. Their free-living relatives are still out there, which is what makes it possible to compare them with the organelles in Step 9.

CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Free-living, or not?

Is a cyanobacterium a chloroplast?

No. A cyanobacterium is a whole free-living bacterium. A chloroplast is an organelle inside a eukaryotic cell that descends from one.

Which of the two bacteria could already photosynthesize before it was engulfed?

The cyanobacterium. That ability is what the host gained when it kept one.

Those are the cells. Where do they sit on the tree of life?
STEP 4 · THE BIG PICTURE

Two events on the tree of life

Endosymbiosis has been fundamentally important to the origin of eukaryotes. Now that you have met the cells, see where the story sits on the tree of life: two separate events, each one a line of bacteria joining a line of eukaryotes and staying.2

INTERACTIVE · THE TREE OF LIFE, AND TWO LINEAGES THAT MOVED IN

THE TREE OF LIFEThree domains, and one of them is oursEvery living thing belongs to one of three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes. Read the tree from the root to the tips: time runs that way, and every tip is alive today.Animals and plants are twigs on a single branch, the eukaryotes (boxed). Mitochondria and chloroplasts are found only on that branch.
EVENT 1 · GAVE RISE TO MITOCHONDRIAA line of bacteria joins the stem of the eukaryotesFollow the amber line. It leaves the alpha-proteobacteria branch and meets the eukaryote stem at the flashing dot. That meeting is the engulfing, about 2 billion years ago.2The dot sits on the stem before the point where today's eukaryote groups split apart. So the amber line then runs up every one of those branches: all eukaryotes inherited mitochondria.
EVENT 2 · GAVE RISE TO CHLOROPLASTSA second line of bacteria joins one eukaryote branchFollow the green line. It leaves the cyanobacteria branch and meets just one eukaryote branch, the one leading to plants and other photosynthetic eukaryotes.It joins after the split, so only that branch carries it. Animals and fungi are on other branches and never had chloroplasts. The cell it joined already carried the amber line, so mitochondria came first.
WHAT THE LINES MEANNothing jumped. A lineage moved in and has been inherited ever sinceA bacterium did not turn into a eukaryote, and it did not hop from one domain to another. One bacterium was taken inside a host cell and kept dividing there. Each time the host cell divided, its daughter cells received some of them. That has continued, without a break, to this day.So every mitochondrion in you is a direct descendant of that one engulfed bacterium. The two white rings mark the common ancestors: from there, one line stayed free-living and leads to today's bacteria, and the other went inside and leads to today's organelles. They are relatives.Each event belongs to a branch, at one point along it. Everything that descends from that point inherited the organelle. Event 1 sits below the branching point of the living eukaryotes, Event 2 above it.

A simplified tree. Only the branches that matter for this story are named, and branch lengths mean nothing.

THE TWO EVENTS

This part is organized around them

EVENT 1An alpha-proteobacterium gave rise to mitochondria. Every eukaryote descends from the cell that gained them.
EVENT 2A cyanobacterium gave rise to chloroplasts. All photosynthetic eukaryotes have them.
ONE THING TO HOLD ON TOPhotosynthetic eukaryotes are not only plants. A large share of them are not plants at all. Step 7 comes back to this.
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Read it off the tree

The tree suggests that organelles in eukaryotes arose from: archaea, bacteria, or other eukaryotes?

Bacteria. Both colored lines start on the bacterial branch. Neither starts from the archaea, and neither starts from another eukaryote.

Why do animals have mitochondria but no chloroplasts?

Event 1 happened on the stem of the eukaryotes, before they split into today's groups, so every eukaryote inherited mitochondria. Event 2 happened on one branch only, and animals are not on it.

Did a bacterium jump into the eukaryote domain?

No. One bacterium was engulfed and its descendants have been passed down inside eukaryotic cells ever since. Its free-living relatives are still bacteria today.

That is the map. Now the idea that explains it.
STEP 5 · THE IDEA

One cell living inside another

Symbiosis is a close interaction between species that has evolved over a long time. Endosymbiosis is a symbiosis in which one species lives inside the other.1,2

THE THEORY OF ENDOSYMBIOSIS Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria. They were engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells and became a permanent part of them.

Lynn Margulis championed this theory. Endosymbiosis has been fundamentally important to the origin of eukaryotes.

ancestral
eukaryotic cellfree-living
bacteriumone cell, the bacterium
living on inside it
FOUR WORDS, ONE DRAWING

Symbiosis, symbiont, endosymbiosis, endosymbiont

SYMBIOSISENDOSYMBIOSISsymbiontsymbiontclose togetherhostendosymbiontone inside the other
SYMBIOSISA close interaction between species that has evolved over a long time.2
SYMBIONTAn organism that lives in that kind of closely evolved association with another species.1
ENDOSYMBIOSISA symbiosis in which one species lives inside the other.
ENDOSYMBIONTThe one living inside. The cell it lives in is the host.
WHO HAD THE IDEA

An old idea that had to wait for its evidence

early 1900s1967DNA sequencingthe ideanew evidencethe decisive test
1Konstantin Merezhkovsky, more than a century ago
He saw that chloroplasts closely resemble cyanobacteria, and he knew that corals keep algae inside their tissues as symbionts. He put the two together: chloroplasts began as symbiotic cyanobacteria. With the tools of the time it could not be tested, and it was set aside, more neglected than disproved.1
2Lynn Margulis, 1967
She brought the idea back and supported it with new kinds of data from cell and molecular biology, including what the electron microscope showed inside chloroplasts.
3Then DNA could be read
Chloroplasts and mitochondria turned out to have DNA of their own. Comparing its sequence with bacterial DNA was the decisive test. Step 9 lets you do both checks yourself.
That is the idea. Here is what actually happened, in order.
STEP 6 · WHAT HAPPENED

Two engulfing events, in order

The host did not start out with mitochondria or chloroplasts. It gained them one at a time, by engulfing a bacterium and keeping it.2

WHO IS THE HOST? The host is the cell that did the engulfing: an ancestral eukaryotic cell. In Event 1 the host had no mitochondria yet. In Event 2 the host was one of its descendants, a eukaryotic cell that already had mitochondria.
THE TIMELINE
ABOUT 2 BILLION YEARS AGO · EVENT 1Ancestral eukaryotic cell (the host) + alpha-proteobacteriumThe alpha-proteobacterium becomes the mitochondrion.
LATER · EVENT 2Eukaryotic cell with mitochondria (the host) + cyanobacteriumThe cyanobacterium becomes the chloroplast.
TODAYThe descendantsAll eukaryotes descend from the cell that gained mitochondria. Plants and some algae carry chloroplasts from Event 2 as well.
Membrane of the host, the ancestral eukaryotic cell Nucleus Alpha-proteobacterium, then mitochondrion Cyanobacterium, then chloroplast

The frames are a simplified model. Nobody watched these events happen, which is why Step 9 is about evidence. The host is drawn with a nucleus, although whether the nucleus arose before or after this event is not resolved (Step 12).

EVENT 1 · ABOUT 2 BILLION YEARS AGO

The alpha-proteobacterium moves in

1The host, an ancestral eukaryotic cell with no mitochondria, meets a free-living alpha-proteobacterium.
2The host engulfs it, most likely as prey: a predator swallowing its food.
3It is not digested. It survives inside the host.
4Over a very long time it becomes the mitochondrion.
RESULT OF EVENT 1

A eukaryotic cell with mitochondria

The two became obligate mutualists: neither can live without the other. The bacterium is now an endosymbiont, a symbiont living inside its host. Every eukaryote alive today descends from this cell.

EVENT 2 · LATER

The cyanobacterium moves in

1A descendant of that cell, which already has mitochondria, meets a free-living cyanobacterium.
2The host engulfs it.
3It survives inside the host too.
4Over a very long time it becomes the chloroplast.
RESULT OF EVENT 2

A eukaryotic cell with mitochondria and chloroplasts

This cell can photosynthesize, because its chloroplasts can. Plants and some algae descend from it. Taking in a bacterium like this is called primary endosymbiosis: an engulfing (phagocytic) eukaryote became a photosynthetic eukaryote, a green alga.

WHAT IT BECAME

An obligate mutualism

Host:
eukaryotic
cell
protection + resourcesenergy the host can use
Engulfed bacterium

Over evolutionary time the two became more and more integrated, until neither could live without the other. Today the host supplies protection and resources, and the organelle supplies energy the host can use.

THE ORDER

Mitochondria came first

Mitochondriathen chloroplasts

How we know: the cyanobacteriumⓘPhotosynthetic bacteria. The group that chloroplasts descended from. was engulfed by a cell that already had mitochondria. That is why mitochondria are found right across the eukaryotes, but only photosynthetic ones have chloroplasts as well.

Two events, two new organelles. What did that lead to?
STEP 7 · WHAT IT BECAME

From those two events to you and to plants

Follow the host cell forward. One branch of its descendants stopped after Event 1. Another went through Event 2 as well.2

THE STARTThe host: an ancestral eukaryotic cellNo mitochondria and no chloroplasts yet.
Event 1 · engulfs an alpha-proteobacterium
AFTER EVENT 1A eukaryotic cell with mitochondriaThe ancestor of every eukaryote alive today.
No second event
TODAY · MITOCHONDRIA ONLYAnimals and fungiYour own cells are here: a nucleus and mitochondria, no chloroplasts.
Event 2 · engulfs a cyanobacterium
TODAY · MITOCHONDRIA AND CHLOROPLASTSPlants and some algaeA plant cell has both: mitochondria from Event 1 and chloroplasts from Event 2.

So the cell with both organelles is the end of the story, not the start. Cyanobacteria themselves are still around too: they are photosynthetic, but they are bacteria, not plants. Other groups of algae got their chloroplasts in a more roundabout way, which is beyond this module.

STRAIGHT OUT OF EVENT 2

Red algae, green algae, and then land plants

common ancestorafter Event 2red algaegreen algaeland plants

The engulfing of a cyanobacterium happened in a common ancestor of the green algae and the red algae. Both groups inherited its chloroplasts. Land plants arose later, from among the green algae, and carry the same chloroplasts.1

Their chloroplasts are wrapped in two membranes, which is what an engulfed cyanobacterium would leave behind.

IT HAPPENED AGAIN

A second, separate case: Paulinella chromatophora

its chloroplasts20 µma photosynthetic
amoeba
WHAT IT ISA photosynthetic amoeba, a single-celled eukaryote.
WHAT IS DIFFERENTIts chloroplast came from a different branch of the cyanobacteria than the one that gave rise to every other chloroplast. It is a separate engulfing, and a more recent one.
WHY BIOLOGISTS CAREIts chloroplast still holds about one-third to one-half of the ancestral cyanobacterial genome. That suggests the change from bacterium to organelle is still in progress in this organism.1
HOW MUCH OF THE CYANOBACTERIAL GENOME IS STILL IN THE CHLOROPLAST
Paulinella's chloroplast
About one-third to one-half of the ancestral genome.
Chloroplasts of plants and algae
60 to 200 genes, out of the 2000 to 3000 in their closest cyanobacterial relatives.
KEEP THE TWO APART Event 2 on the tree is the old one, in the ancestor of red and green algae. It is the one that explains plants. Paulinella is a separate, later event in one amoeba. It shows that endosymbiosis is not a one-time accident.

Chloroplasts turn up on many separate branches. Diatoms, brown algae, dinoflagellates and euglenids all photosynthesize, and none of them is a plant. Most photosynthetic eukaryotes are algae, many of them single cells.

All of these groups have mitochondria, green or not. Apicomplexans are marked green because they still carry a leftover chloroplast, although they no longer photosynthesize.

So what do those two organelles look like today?
STEP 8 · THE TWO ORGANELLES TODAY

What to notice in each one

Both still carry clear signs of where they came from: their own DNA and more than one membrane.2

MITOCHONDRION

The cell's power supply

outer membraneinner membrane, foldedits own circular DNA
WHAT IT DOESCellular respiration. It makes most of the ATP that powers cellular functions.
WHERE IT CAME FROMA free-living alpha-proteobacterium.
WHAT TO NOTICETwo membranes, its own circular DNA, and it divides by binary fission.
CHLOROPLAST

The cell's solar panel

outer membraneinner membraneits own circular DNAstacks that capture light
WHAT IT DOESPhotosynthesis. It captures light energy and converts it into chemical energy.
WHERE IT CAME FROMA free-living cyanobacterium.
WHAT TO NOTICETwo or more membranes, its own circular DNA, and it divides by binary fission.

Each organelle has an outer and an inner membrane. Having two membranes, or more, is what you would expect of something that was once taken inside another cell.

That is the story. Nobody watched it happen, so how do we know it is true?
STEP 9 · HOW DO WE KNOW?

Testing the theory: five predictions

Nobody watched any of this happen. So the theory is tested the way any claim about the past is tested: if it is true, what should we still be able to see today?2

THE LOGIC OF THIS STEP
1The claim
Mitochondria and chloroplasts used to be free-living bacteria.
2The prediction
Then they should still look, behave and test like bacteria, even though they sit inside a eukaryotic cell.
3The check
Five things to look at. Each one below is a prediction, then what we actually find.
FIVE CLUES · FROM THE WEAKEST TO THE MOST CONVINCING
CLUE 1Sizeabout the size of bacteria
CLUE 2Own DNAcircular, like a bacterium’s
CLUE 3Divisionby binary fission
CLUE 4Membranestwo or more
CLUE 5DNA sequencesnest inside bacterial groups
WEAKEST
MOST CONVINCING
PREDICTION 1 OF 5
1

Size

RESEMBLANCE · THE WEAKEST CLUE
alpha-proteobacteriummitochondrion≈cyanobacteriumchloroplast≈
IF THEY WERE ONCE BACTERIA, WE WOULD EXPECTAn organelle that used to be a bacterium should be about the size of one.
WHAT WE FINDMitochondria are about the size of alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplasts are about the size of cyanobacteria.
SOIt fits. On its own this is the weakest clue, since plenty of things are small.
PREDICTION 2 OF 5
2

Their own circular DNA

RESEMBLANCE
bacteriummitochondrionchloroplastnucleusCIRCULAR DNAa closed loop, no endsLINEAR DNAstrands with ends
IF THEY WERE ONCE BACTERIA, WE WOULD EXPECTA former bacterium should have brought its own DNA along, packaged the way bacteria package it: as a circle.
WHAT WE FINDEach organelle carries its own genome, separate from the DNA in the nucleus, and it is a circular molecule. The cell's own chromosomes, in the nucleus, are not loops.
SOIt fits. There is bacterial-style DNA sitting inside a eukaryotic cell, and only inside these two organelles.
PREDICTION 3 OF 5
3

Binary fission

RESEMBLANCE
a bacteriuma mitochondriona chloroplastonecopies its DNApinches in twotwothe cell itself · mitosis, a different processchromosomes line uppulled apart
IF THEY WERE ONCE BACTERIA, WE WOULD EXPECTA former bacterium should still reproduce the way bacteria do. Bacteria divide by binary fission. Eukaryotic cells do not: they divide by mitosis and meiosis.
WHAT WE FINDMitochondria and chloroplasts multiply by binary fission. Their DNA is copied, then the organelle pinches in two.
SOIt fits. The cell around them divides one way, and these two parts keep dividing the other way, the bacterial way. They still reproduce like the bacteria they once were.
PREDICTION 4 OF 5
4

Two or more membranes

RESEMBLANCE
1A bacterium sits against the membrane of the host, the ancestral eukaryotic cell.
2The host's membrane folds inward around it.
3The fold pinches off. The bacterium is now inside the host, enclosed in membrane.
The bacterium The host's membrane (the eukaryotic cell's)

In the standard picture, the host's membrane wraps around the bacterium as it is taken in and becomes the organelle's outer membrane, while the bacterium's own membrane becomes the inner one. The real history is more complicated than a cartoon, so remember the number: two or more.

IF THEY WERE ONCE BACTERIA, WE WOULD EXPECTA cell that was taken inside another cell should end up wrapped in more than one membrane.
WHAT WE FINDMitochondria and chloroplasts are wrapped in two membranes, or more.
SOIt fits. More than one membrane is consistent with an engulfing event. One membrane of its own, plus one from the host that wrapped around it.
PREDICTION 5 OF 5
5

DNA sequences

DESCENT · THE MOST CONVINCING
other bacteriaan alpha-proteobacteriumMITOCHONDRIAL DNAan alpha-proteobacteriuma cyanobacteriumCHLOROPLAST DNAa cyanobacteriumthe same cell's nuclear DNASIMPLIFIED TREE
IF THEY WERE ONCE BACTERIA, WE WOULD EXPECTThis is the sharpest test. If mitochondria descended from alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria, their DNA sequences should group with those bacteria on a family tree.
WHAT WE FINDThey do. Mitochondrial DNA nests inside the alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplast DNA nests inside the cyanobacteria.
SOThe first four show a resemblance to bacteria. This one shows descent, and it names the exact groups. That is why it is the most convincing, and why it settled the question.

SAMPLE 2 · A CHLOROPLAST FROM A RED ALGAThe same parallel membranes, inside a eukaryotic cellThis is not a cell. It is one organelle from inside the cell of a red alga, and it is packed with the same kind of parallel membrane.
SAMPLE 3 · A CHLOROPLAST FROM A PLANTParallel membranes again, here gathered into stacksA plant chloroplast. The membranes are parallel here too, with many of them piled into stacks.What the microscope shows: the likeness between chloroplasts and cyanobacteria goes all the way down to the fine detail of how the photosynthetic membranes are arranged.

These are drawings of what the micrographs show, not photographs. Each view has its own scale bar, as micrographs do. Compare the pattern inside, not the sizes.

HOW STRONG IS THIS? It is a resemblance, like the first four clues, only much finer. It made the old idea worth taking seriously again. It did not settle it. The DNA did.
TRY IT · READ THE DNA YOURSELF

Whose gene does the organelle's gene look like?

THE POINT OF THIS TEST · TWO COMPARISONS, ONE CONCLUSION
organelle's gene≈a free-living bacterium's gene
Comparison 1: are they alike? If yes, the organelle's gene is a bacterial gene.
organelle's gene≠the gene in its own cell's nucleus
Comparison 2: are they different? If yes, the organelle's gene is not one of the cell's own.
SOLike a bacterium, and unlike the cell it lives in. The organelle was not built by the cell around it: it came in from outside, as a bacterium.1

The gene compared is the one for the small ribosomal RNA. Every cell has it, and it is the gene the textbook's figure uses. Three real copies of it are lined up: the organelle's, a free-living bacterium's, and the one in the nucleus of the same plant, thale cress.6–10

For reference, against a cyanobacterium, a different kind of bacterium: about 71 of every 100 lined-up letters match, and 12 of every 100 ten-letter stretches are shared. The same ranking, by a smaller margin, which is why researchers do not stop at counting. The gray stretches are places where this plant's mitochondrial gene has extra letters with nothing to line up against.
How these numbers were produced and checked

The data are real. The sequences are public records in the NCBI Nucleotide database, linked under Sources at the end of this part.11 They were downloaded twice, on different days, and the two downloads are identical.

How the letters were lined up. With the standard method for aligning two whole sequences, global alignment12,13, scoring +1 for a match, −1 for a mismatch, −10 to open a gap and −1 to extend one.

Why a chance level is shown. Any two strings of A, C, G and T match at some positions. To measure that, each comparison was repeated 20 times with the other gene's letters shuffled into random order. Shuffled genes still score about 40 per 100. So only the part of a score above about 40 means anything.

The second check counts 10-letter stretches shared exactly. It needs no lining up, and chance alone gives almost none.

What was verified. The colored letters on this page were recounted and equal the printed numbers. The ranking, own group of bacteria first and nucleus last, came out the same under three different sets of scoring settings.

What this cannot do. This gene changes slowly, so any two bacteria share much of it. Showing that mitochondria belong inside the alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplasts inside the cyanobacteria takes a family tree built from many species. That is what the original studies did14,15, and it is the conclusive evidence.

WHAT THE SEQUENCES SHOW An organelle's genes are bacterial genes. They match free-living bacteria far better than they match the nucleus of their own cell. Family trees built from sequences like these place mitochondria among the alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplasts among the cyanobacteria.14,15
PUT TOGETHER

Five for five

Size, DNA, division and membranes: four signs that these organelles look and act like bacteria living inside a cell. DNA sequences: which bacteria they came from. Every prediction the theory makes checks out.

STEP 10 · AFTER A VERY LONG TIME TOGETHER

Where did the genes go?

Engulfing a bacterium was only the beginning. Chloroplasts and mitochondria have far fewer genes than the free-living bacteria they came from: thousands of genes became dozens. So where did the rest of each genome go?1,2

CHART · NUMBER OF GENES, DRAWN TO ONE SCALE

2000 to 3000 genes.
Chloroplasts
60 to 200 genes.

0100020003000 GENES

Alpha-proteobacteria, like cyanobacteria, have thousands of genes. The sources give no exact figure for them, so they are left off the chart.1,2

EVERY SQUARE IS ONE GENE PRODUCT

All that a human mitochondrion still codes for

13 proteins 24 RNAs

That is the whole list. The bacterium it descends from needed thousands of genes to live on its own. Many of them migrated to the nucleus, where they still reside.1

INTERACTIVE · FOUR VIEWS OF ONE CELL

Three things that happened to the missing genes, and what came of it

Tap the buttons, or Next route, to click through all 4
nucleuschloroplastno longer needed: losta nuclear gene
does that jobthe chloroplast breaks openits DNA spillsa virus carries DNA acrossgene in the nucleusprotein sent back
ROUTE 1 · LOSTSome genes were simply no longer neededA free-living bacterium has to make everything for itself. Inside a host cell it does not. If a similar gene in the nucleus could already supply what the chloroplast required, the chloroplast's own copy could be lost with no harm done.So these genes were not mislaid. Living inside another cell made them unnecessary, and over time they disappeared. The textbook is careful here: it says some genes may simply have been lost this way.1
ROUTE 2 · MOVED WHEN AN ORGANELLE BROKEDNA spilled out and ended up in the nucleusWhen a chloroplast broke open, its DNA was released inside the host cell, and some of it ended up in the nucleus.Many genes were transported to the nucleus this way.
ROUTE 3 · MOVED ON A VIRUSSome genes hitched a rideViruses carry genetic material from place to place. Some chloroplast genes reached the nucleus by hitching a ride with them.The textbook names this as a second route to the nucleus, alongside Route 2. It is not the only way genes moved, and the textbook gives no further detail on it.
AFTER THE MOVEMany of the moved genes still serve the organelleThe nuclear genome of the flowering plant Arabidopsis contains several thousand genes of cyanobacterial origin. Some of them code for proteins that are made by the host cell and then used inside the chloroplast.1So the chloroplast now depends on genes it no longer carries. Mitochondria tell the same story: many genes from the original bacterial endosymbiont migrated to the nucleus, where they still reside.

Drawn for a chloroplast. A simplified picture: one chloroplast and a few genes stand in for many.

THE SHORT ANSWER

Two fates

SOME MIGRATEDThey moved to the nucleus of the eukaryotic host, and many still work from there.
OTHERS WERE LOSTThey were not needed in the new environment inside a cell.
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Say it in your own words

A chloroplast has 60 to 200 genes. Its closest free-living relatives have 2000 to 3000. Were the missing genes all destroyed?

No. Many moved to the nucleus, where they still exist and often still make proteins for the chloroplast. Others were lost because the host cell already supplied what they provided.

Is a virus the way genes got to the nucleus?

It is one way. The textbook names two: genes were transported when chloroplasts broke, or by hitching a ride with viruses.

If every eukaryote inherited mitochondria, what about the few that have none?
STEP 11 · THE EXCEPTION THAT IS NOT ONE

Eukaryotes with no mitochondria

Most eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria, but a few single-celled eukaryotes that live in oxygen-free environments do not. Does that break the rule that all eukaryotes have them? Biologists had two ways to explain these cells.1

INTERACTIVE · TWO HYPOTHESES, ONE PIECE OF EVIDENCE

Never had them, or lost them?

still in the nucleus
THE FIRST HYPOTHESISThey branched off before mitochondria existedBiologists originally thought these eukaryotes were leftovers from a time before Event 1: cells with a nucleus that had never taken in the bacterium.That proposal was abandoned. These cells turned out to have genes in their nucleus that migrated there from the mitochondrial symbiont. A cell that never had the symbiont could not have its genes.
THE SUPPORTED HYPOTHESISThey had mitochondria once, and lost themThe textbook reports that every mitochondria-free eukaryote examined has relict mitochondrial genes in its nuclear genome (the amber dots).1So their ancestors went through Event 1 like every other eukaryote. These organisms live in oxygen-free environments, and over time their mitochondria were lost or, as the next drawing shows, altered to suit life without oxygen.
INTERACTIVE · WHAT IS LEFT OF THE MITOCHONDRION

From mitochondrion to remnant

Tap the buttons, or Next organelle, to click through all 3
genes of
mitochondrial origin,
in the nucleusmakes ATP using oxygenits own small genomemakes ATP without oxygenlittle or no DNAproteinsmakes no ATP at alla remnant
WHERE IT STARTSA mitochondrionThe organelle most eukaryotic cells have. It carries out aerobic cellular respiration, and it still has a small genome of its own, with many more of its genes in the nucleus.
ALTERED · IN MANY EUKARYOTES THAT LACK MITOCHONDRIAA hydrogenosomeA small organelle that generates ATP by anaerobic processes, without oxygen. It has little or no DNA.The giveaway is in the nucleus: genes of mitochondrial origin, coding for proteins that work inside the hydrogenosome. So hydrogenosomes appear to be highly altered mitochondria, adapted to life where oxygen is scarce.1
REDUCED FURTHER · IN OTHER ANAEROBIC EUKARYOTESA mitosomeA still smaller organelle that also appears to be a remnant mitochondrion. It has lost all capacity for metabolism, so it makes no ATP.It does retain the genes needed to assemble the clusters of iron and sulfur found in many proteins. Why those genes in particular are kept remains unknown.

A sketch. The sources say hydrogenosomes are small and mitosomes smaller still, and give no measurements.

SO WHAT DO WE CONCLUDE?

Mitochondria are a universal feature of all eukaryotes

had mitochondriamoved to a place with no oxygenlost or reduced themtheir genes are still in the nucleus

The few eukaryotes without mitochondria most likely lost them at some point in their evolutionary history, and they still have mitochondrial genes in the nuclear genome. For that reason mitochondria still count as a universal feature of all eukaryotes.2

Put precisely, what every eukaryote shares is the ancestry: each one descends from a cell that had mitochondria, even where the organelle itself has since been reduced or lost.

Universal for eukaryotes, not for all life: bacteria and archaea never had mitochondria.

One step beyond the textbook: a eukaryote with no trace of the organelle

In 2016 researchers reported a single-celled eukaryote from the gut of a chinchilla, Monocercomonoides, that has no mitochondrion of any kind and none of the hallmark mitochondrial proteins.16 Its close relatives still have small mitochondria, so it lost the organelle rather than never having one.

That is why the ancestry wording above is the careful one. For an exam, use the statement in the box: mitochondria are treated as a universal feature of all eukaryotes.

That much is known. Here is what is not.
STEP 12 · WHERE THE EVIDENCE RUNS OUT

Still open: the origin of the eukaryotic cell itself

If mitochondria began as proteobacteria and chloroplasts as cyanobacteria, where did the rest of the eukaryotic cell come from? This is where settled science ends and active research begins.1

WHAT IS IN A EUKARYOTE'S NUCLEUS

Genes from four different sources

from the bacterial symbionts from other bacteria found only in eukaryotes related to archaea
FROM THE SYMBIONTSThe genes that migrated out of the mitochondrion and the chloroplast.
FROM OTHER BACTERIAPicked up at many points in evolutionary history by horizontal gene transfer.
ONLY IN EUKARYOTESApparently evolved after the eukaryote domain originated.
RELATED TO ARCHAEAIncluding the genes used to transcribe DNA and translate it into proteins.

The drawing shows that the four sources are mixed together. It does not show how many genes come from each.1

THE CLOSEST RELATIVES OF THE HOST

The Asgard archaea

an archaeon: no nucleusarm-like projections, function unknown
2015The genome of an archaeon from hot springs on the floor of the Arctic Ocean was pieced together. It turned out to be a close relative of eukaryotic cells, with genes like those that organize the inside of a eukaryotic cell.1
SINCE THENSimilar archaea were soon found in many environments around the world, and are now grouped as the Asgard archaea. By 2021 more than 600 kinds had been identified, and one had been grown in the laboratory.
WHAT IT SUGGESTSIncreasing evidence suggests that the cell which took in the ancestor of mitochondria was descended from archaea of this kind. So it seems likely that some portion of the eukaryotic cell is archaeal.
INTERACTIVE · TWO HYPOTHESES FOR THE ORIGIN OF THE EUKARYOTIC CELL

Which came first: the nucleus, or the symbiosis?

Tap a button to explore
HYPOTHESIS 1 · NUCLEUS FIRSTarchaeonnucleus formsengulfs iteukaryoteHYPOTHESIS 2 · SYMBIOSIS FIRSTarchaeonmoves innucleus formseukaryote
HYPOTHESIS 1The host was already a true eukaryoteIn this view the archaeal ancestor had already changed enormously before it met the bacterium. It had a nucleus, a cytoskeleton and an internal membrane system, but only a limited ability to get energy out of organic molecules.Then it engulfed a proteobacterium capable of aerobic respiration, which became the mitochondrion.The difficulty: no one has ever found a eukaryote that does not have, and never had, mitochondria.1
HYPOTHESIS 2There was no eukaryotic cell before mitochondriaIn this view the eukaryotic cell as a whole began as a symbiosis between an archaeon and a proteobacterium.The proteobacterium became the mitochondrion and gave many genes to the nuclear genome. The archaeon gave others, including the genes for transcribing DNA and translating it into proteins. The nucleus came afterwards.
TAP A HYPOTHESISSame ingredients, same result, different orderBoth hypotheses start with an archaeon and a proteobacterium and end with a eukaryote that has mitochondria. They disagree about which came first: the nucleus, or the symbiosis.
WHAT BOTH EXPLAINWhy the eukaryotic genome is a hybrid, with some genes like those of bacteria and others like those of archaea.
WHAT NEITHER FULLY EXPLAINSThe origin of the nucleus, of linear chromosomes, of the eukaryotic cytoskeleton, or of a cytoplasm divided up by membranes.
WHAT TO HOLD ON TO How and when the nucleus of eukaryotic cells first originated is not resolved. It is still an active area of research, and one of biology's deepest unanswered questions.1,2
A NOTE ON WORDS This part calls the host an ancestral eukaryotic cell. Under Hypothesis 2 it was still an archaeon at the moment of engulfing. Both describe the same cell: the one that took in the bacterium.
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Without looking back

What are the two hypotheses for the origin of the eukaryotic cell?

One: an archaeal ancestor first became a true eukaryotic cell, with a nucleus, and only later engulfed the proteobacterium that became the mitochondrion. Two: the eukaryotic cell began as a symbiosis between an archaeon and a proteobacterium, and the nucleus arose afterwards.

Which parts of the story are settled?

That mitochondria descend from alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria. What the host was, and where the nucleus came from, are not.

HOW SURE IS EACH CLAIM?

From settled to still open

Science is not equally sure about every part of this story. Here is where each claim stands.

CONCLUSIVEMitochondria descend from alpha-proteobacteria, chloroplasts from cyanobacteriaDNA sequences place each organelle inside its group of bacteria. This is what settled the theory.
CONSISTENT WITH IT, BUT NOT PROOF ALONESize, circular DNA, binary fission, two or more membranes, matching internal membranesEach is what you would expect of a former bacterium. Each could in principle have another explanation, which is why they count as support.
STRONGLY SUPPORTEDEukaryotes without mitochondria once had themEvery one examined so far still carries mitochondrial genes in its nucleus.
STATED WITH CAUTIONExactly how each gene left the organelleSome genes moved to the nucleus. Others, in the textbook's words, may simply have been lost. The broad picture is clear, the route taken by each gene is not.
NOT RESOLVEDWhat kind of cell the host was, and how and when the nucleus aroseTwo competing hypotheses, and neither explains everything. This is an active area of research.

Lock it in · Part 1

  1. A bacterial cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts. Most of its DNA is one circular chromosome, and it divides by binary fission.
  2. Mitochondria descended from free-living alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplasts descended from free-living cyanobacteria. Each was engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell and became an obligate mutualist living inside it: an endosymbiont.
  3. Mitochondria came first. The cyanobacterium was engulfed by a cell that already had mitochondria.
  4. Nothing jumped between domains. The engulfed bacteria kept dividing inside their hosts and have been inherited ever since.
  5. Mitochondria do cellular respiration. Chloroplasts do photosynthesis. A plant cell has both organelles, so it does both.
  6. Five lines of evidence: size, circular DNA, binary fission, two or more membranes, and DNA sequences.
  7. The conclusive one is the DNA sequences: the organelles' DNA nests inside those bacterial groups.
  8. Thousands of genes became dozens. Some moved to the nucleus, and others were lost because they were not needed inside a cell.
  9. A few eukaryotes have no mitochondria. They lost them, and still carry mitochondrial genes in the nucleus, so mitochondria remain a universal feature of all eukaryotes: every eukaryote descends from a cell that had them.
  10. How and when the nucleus first originated is not resolved. It is still an active area of research.

FROM PART 1 TO PART 2

Why a story about cells ends with wolves

The two parts are one story. Part 1 explains how photosynthesis got into eukaryotes, and how every eukaryote came to have mitochondria. Part 2 follows the energy that primary producers capture as it moves from one organism to another.

EVENT 2 GAVE SOME CELLS CHLOROPLASTSSo they can make food from lightThat is how photosynthesis got into eukaryotes. Plants and algae are primary producers because of it, alongside the cyanobacteria that were already doing it.
EVENT 1 GAVE EVERY EUKARYOTE MITOCHONDRIASo they can release the energy stored in foodProducers and consumers both do this. Consumers cannot make their own food, so they get it from other organisms. That is what a food web arrow records.
+ / +
BOTH EVENTS WERE SPECIES INTERACTIONSA mutualism between a host and a bacteriumPart 2 carries on with species interactions: who eats whom, and how one species reaches another through the web.
Two engulfing eventstwo kinds of cellproducers and consumersfood websone species changes, others follow
PART 2

Food webs

THE QUESTION Some organisms make their own food and the rest get theirs from other organisms. So who eats whom, and what happens to everyone else when one species disappears?

Eleven steps, picking up exactly where Part 1 stopped: who makes food, how to read a chain and a web, how effects travel, how much energy moves up, and why a few species matter far more than the rest.

STEP 1 · FROM PART 1 TO HERE

Two ways to get food

Part 1 ended with two kinds of eukaryotic cell: one with chloroplasts and one without. Among eukaryotes, that difference goes with two ways of getting food.

HAS CHLOROPLASTSIt can make its own foodPlants and algae photosynthesize with their chloroplasts. Cyanobacteria, the bacteria chloroplasts came from, were photosynthesizing long before and still do. All of these are autotrophs.
NO CHLOROPLASTSIt gets its food from other organismsAnimals and fungi cannot make their own. These are heterotrophs.
FOUR PREFIXES THAT DECODE THE VOCABULARY
auto-MEANS “self”Makes its own food.
hetero-MEANS “other”Gets its food from other organisms.
photo-MEANS “light”Gets its energy from light.
chemo-MEANS “chemical”Gets its energy from chemicals.
PUT THEM TOGETHER
PHOTO + AUTO + TROPHA photoautotroph uses light to make its own food: a plant, an alga, a cyanobacterium.
CHEMO + HETERO + TROPHA chemoheterotroph gets both its energy and its food from other organisms: you, an elk, a wolf, a fungus.

Module 2.3 goes further into the different kinds of producer. Here you only need the prefixes.

So some organisms make their own food and the rest get it from other organisms. Put them in order.
STEP 2 · WHO EATS WHOM

A food chain, and what the arrows mean

Line up who eats whom and you get a food chain. Each position has a name.

DIAGRAM · ONE FOOD CHAIN

Grass, elk, wolf

GrassElkWolf
GRASS · PRIMARY PRODUCERMakes its own food. An autotroph. Everything else in the chain depends on it.
ELK · PRIMARY CONSUMEREats producers. In everyday words, a herbivore.
WOLF · SECONDARY CONSUMEREats primary consumers. In everyday words, a carnivore. Whatever eats a secondary consumer is a tertiary consumer.
THE RULE EVERYONE GETS BACKWARDS

Arrows point from the food to the eater

✓
GrassElkWolf
✕
WolfElkGrass

An arrow shows where the energy goes. Energy moves from the organism being eaten into the organism eating it, so that is the way the arrow points.

Module 2.3 follows that energy: how much moves up, and why so little.

One chain is tidy. Real communities are not.
STEP 3 · THE REAL THING

A food web: many chains at once

No community is one neat chain. Most organisms eat more than one thing and are eaten by more than one thing. Draw all of it and you have a food web.

NOW ZOOM OUTThe same ocean, with everyone in itA real community has many more species, and the energy can go in many different directions. Krill alone feed fish, squid, penguins, seals and whales.Still missing from the drawing: decomposers and parasites. They are hugely important, and almost never drawn.

A simplified web. A real one has many more species and many more arrows.

HOW TO READ ANY FOOD WEB

Four things to check

THE ARROWSThey show energy flow. Each one points from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it.
THE BOTTOMWhatever has no arrow coming into it makes its own food. Here that is the phytoplankton: photoautotrophs.
EVERYTHING ELSEChemoheterotrophs. They get their energy and their carbon from what they eat.
WHO IS NOT DRAWNDecomposers and parasites. Both are hugely important, and both are usually left out.
WHY A WEB AND NOT A CHAIN

Energy goes in many directions

In a chain each organism has one food and one predator. In a real community most have several of each, so the energy that enters at the bottom can take many different routes to the top.

Same species, same arrows. Now each row is one trophic level, which makes it easy to answer "where do the wolves go?" and "where do the elk go?"

READ IT OFF THE ROWS

Where each one sits

ELK, DEER, MOOSEPrimary consumers. Everything they eat is in the bottom row.

CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

What should affect the moose population?

Insects? Willows and aspen? Rabbits? Or more than one trophic level?

More than one trophic level. Willows and aspen (the level below) feed moose, and wolves (the level above) eat them. Elk and beaver matter too, because they eat the same plants.

HOW TO WORK OUT ANY ORGANISM'S LEVEL

Count the levels below it

NOTHING BELOW ITPrimary producer. Makes its own food. Trophic level 1.
ONE LEVEL BELOW ITPrimary consumer. Eats producers. Trophic level 2.
TWO LEVELS BELOW ITSecondary consumer. Eats primary consumers. Trophic level 3.
THREE LEVELS BELOW ITTertiary consumer. Eats secondary consumers. Trophic level 4.
IT EATS FROM MORE THAN ONE LEVELTrophic omnivore. It does not sit on a single level.
A CHAIN WITH ALL FOUR
WillowInsectInsect-eating birdHawk

Back to Part 1 for a moment: every green species in the web has chloroplasts from Event 2, and every species in it has mitochondria from Event 1.

The simplified Yellowstone web has no pure secondary or tertiary consumer, because both of its top species eat from two levels. This made-up chain shows what they look like: the bird is secondary, the hawk tertiary.

WATCH THIS DEFINITION

Omnivore does not mean “eats plants and animals” here

In everyday use an omnivore eats both plants and animals. In ecology a trophic omnivore is anything that feeds on two or more trophic levels.

A consumer that eats both primary and secondary consumers is a trophic omnivore even if it never touches a plant. And anything that feeds on a trophic omnivore is classed as one as well.

WHO IS MISSING?

Decomposers and parasites

Decomposers (bacteria, archaea and fungi) feed on the dead remains of every level. Parasites feed on living hosts at every level. Both are usually left out of food web drawings, and both are always there. Parasites come back in Step 11, and decomposers get a module of their own.

Everything in that web is connected. So what happens when one part changes?
STEP 4 · EFFECTS THAT TRAVEL

Direct and indirect effects

Because everything in a web is connected, a change in one species reaches others it never touches.

THE TWO KINDS

How to tell them apart

DIRECT EFFECTBetween two species that interact with each other. One eats the other, for example.
INDIRECT EFFECTBetween two species that do not interact directly. It travels through one or more species in between.

The test: is there a species in the middle? If yes, the effect is indirect.

DIAGRAM · EFFECTS, NOT ENERGY

Foxes help grass without ever touching it

Arctic foxesGeeseLemmingsGrasses−−−−+
Direct effect Indirect effect

These arrows show who affects whom, so they are not food web arrows. Foxes eat geese and lemmings. Geese and lemmings eat grass. More foxes means fewer grazers, which means more grass.

DIAGRAM · AN EFFECT CAN TRAVEL MORE THAN ONE STEP

Follow it down the line

WolvesElkWillowsBeavers−−+indirect +indirect +
STEP BY STEPWolves lower elk (−). Elk lower willows (−). Willows raise beavers (+), because beavers eat willow.
WOLVES → WILLOWSIndirect, and positive. Fewer elk means more willow.
WOLVES → BEAVERSIndirect, and positive again. More willow means more food for beavers.

A handy check on the sign: two negatives in a row make a positive. Wolves hurt elk, elk hurt willows, so wolves help willows.

PRACTICE · DIRECT OR INDIRECT?

Use the Yellowstone web from Step 3

Wolves and elk

Direct. Wolves eat elk. Nothing sits between them.

Willows and moose

Direct. Moose eat willows.

Wolves and aspen

Indirect. Wolves do not eat aspen. The effect runs through elk and moose, which do. More wolves, fewer browsers, more aspen.

Elk and moose

Indirect. Neither eats the other. They affect each other through the willows and aspen they both eat: more elk leaves less for moose.

Insects and songbirds

Direct. Songbirds eat insects.

Willows and songbirds

Indirect. Songbirds do not eat willows. Willows feed insects, and insects feed songbirds.

So what affects moose? Willows and aspen directly, wolves directly, and elk and beaver indirectly. More than one trophic level shapes the moose population.

Now start that change at the very top.
STEP 5 · FROM THE TOP DOWN

Trophic cascades

When a top predator influences the density of species at every trophic level below it, that is a trophic cascade. It is a chain of indirect effects that starts at the top.

INTERACTIVE · ANIMATION · THE WOLVES OF YELLOWSTONE, IN SIX STAGES

From wolves to a river: the story of a cascade

Tap the buttons, or Next stage, to click through all 6
no wolves: elk graze the valley barewolves return: elk leave the valleywillow and aspen grow backsongbirds and beavers move inbeaver ponds: ducks, fish and moreroots hold the banks: the river steadies
STAGE 1 · WITHOUT THE TOP PREDATORElk eat the valley downWith no wolves, elk and deer graze wherever they like, including along the rivers. Young willow and aspen are eaten before they can grow. The banks are bare.
STAGE 2 · TOP DOWNThe wolves change how the elk behaveWolves kill some elk. Just as important, the elk change their behavior: they stay out of the valleys and gorges where they are easy to catch.This is a top-down effect. It starts at the top of the food web and works its way down.
STAGE 3 · ONE LEVEL FURTHER DOWNThe plants regenerateWhere the elk no longer browse, willow and aspen grow back and the trees grow tall. Primary production goes up in exactly the places the elk now avoid.Wolves never touch a tree. This is an indirect effect.
STAGE 4 · OTHER SPECIES FOLLOWSongbirds and beavers move inMore trees means nesting places and food, so songbirds return. More willow means food and building material for beavers, and beavers build dams.
STAGE 5 · AN ENGINEER TAKES OVERThe cascade keeps spreadingBeavers are the classic ecosystem engineer: a dam turns a stream into a pond, and a pond is a home for ducks, fish and other animals.The effects keep branching. This is why it is said that wolves give life to many others.
STAGE 6 · EVEN THE PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHYThe story ends at the river itselfRegenerating forest stabilizes the banks. Roots hold the soil, so there is less erosion, and the river settles into a steadier channel.As the story is told, a predator changed the behavior of its prey, which changed the plants, which changed the shape of the land. This last link is the hardest to show, and how much of it is down to wolves is debated.

This is the story as it is usually told, and it shows what a trophic cascade means. In the real park other things matter as well, and how large the wolf effect is remains debated.

WHAT TO TAKE FROM THE STORY

One predator, five kinds of change

IT IS TOP-DOWNThe change starts with the top predator and travels down the food web.
BEHAVIOR, NOT ONLY NUMBERSThe elk did not just become fewer. They avoided the places where wolves could catch them.
PRIMARY PRODUCTION WENT UPWhere the elk stopped browsing, plants regrew. A predator raised production two levels below it.
OTHER SPECIES MOVED INSongbirds, then beavers, an ecosystem engineer, whose ponds made room for still more species.
THE LAND ITSELF CHANGEDIn this account, regrown vegetation held the soil and the banks, so there was less erosion and the rivers steadied.
THE NEXT QUESTION

So where do wolves sit in the food web?

Go back to the tidied-up web in Step 3. Wolves are at the top, feeding on the level below, and on berries too. The elk and deer are primary consumers. The willows and aspen are primary producers. The cascade ran down through exactly those three rows.

YELLOWSTONE WITHOUT WOLVES
✕Wolves
The top predator is gone.
↑Elk
More elk, grazing wherever they like.
↓Willows and aspen
Eaten down.
YELLOWSTONE WITH WOLVES BACK
↑Wolves
The top predator returns.
↓Elk
Fewer elk, and warier ones.
↑Willows and aspen
They recover.

This is the simplified version of the Yellowstone example. In the real park other things matter as well, such as other predators, water and climate, and how large the wolf effect is remains debated.

HOW DO YOU KNOW IT IS A TROPHIC CASCADE?

Three things to check

1It starts at the top
The change begins with a top predator: it arrives, disappears, or changes in number.
2It reaches every level below
Not only the predator's prey, but what the prey eats too.
3The direction usually flips at each level
In a simple chain: predator up, prey down, producers up. Or the reverse.

If the change starts with a producer or a primary consumer, it is not a trophic cascade, even if other species are affected.

CHART · THE SHAPE OF THE CHANGE

Each level moves the opposite way

Wolves
no wolves
wolves back
Elk
no wolves
wolves back
Willows and aspen
no wolves
wolves back

Bar length stands for abundance. This shows the pattern of a cascade, not measured data.

PRACTICE · CASCADE OR NOT?

Run the three checks

Sea otters disappear. Sea urchins multiply. Kelp forests are grazed away.

Trophic cascade. It starts with a top predator (otters), reaches the producers (kelp), and flips at each level: otters down, urchins up, kelp down.

A wet year grows more grass. Rabbits increase.

Not a cascade. The change starts at the bottom, with a producer. Nothing here begins with a top predator.

A disease kills most of the elk. Willows grow back.

Not a cascade. Willows do benefit indirectly, but the change starts with a primary consumer, not with the top predator.

Wolves return. Elk decline and avoid risky spots. Willows and aspen recover.

Trophic cascade. Top predator, every level below, direction flipping each time.

NOT ONLY NUMBERS

Behavior counts too

Wolves do not just lower the number of elk. Elk also change how they behave: with wolves around they spend less time feeding in places where they are easy to catch. Less browsing there lets the willows and aspen grow back.

TWO DIAGRAMS, TWO JOBS

A cascade diagram is not a food web

FOOD WEBShows who eats whom. Arrows follow the energy.
CASCADE DIAGRAMShows how abundance changes level by level, starting from the top predator.

If there are trophic omnivores in the web, a cascade is hard to predict. You would need data on how strong the direct and indirect effects are.

One more interaction, to test what an arrow means.
STEP 6 · A CASE TO TEST YOURSELF ON

The tree shrew and the pitcher plant

A tree shrew sits on a pitcher plant, feeds on the nectar it makes, and leaves its droppings in the pitcher. Two questions: at what trophic level is the plant, and what kind of interaction is this?

DIAGRAM · WHO GIVES WHAT

Food one way, nitrogen the other

lightnectar:
food for
the shrewdroppings:
nitrogen for
the plantpitcher planttree shrew
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Two questions

At what trophic level is the pitcher plant?

Primary producer. It is a plant: it makes its own food by photosynthesis. What it takes from the droppings is nitrogen, a nutrient, not its energy.

What kind of interaction is this?

Mutualism, the + / + interaction from Module 2.1. The shrew gets food. The plant gets nitrogen. Both benefit.

WHY IT IS HERE

Not every arrow is "who eats whom"

THE SHREWGets energy: nectar is food.
THE PLANTGets a nutrient: nitrogen, which is scarce where it grows. Its energy still comes from light.
So who eats whom, and who helps whom. Now, how much energy is there at each level?
STEP 7 · HOW MUCH ENERGY IS AT EACH LEVEL

Trophic pyramids: pyramids of energy

Stack the trophic levels and make each bar as wide as the energy that level holds. The result always has the same shape.

DIAGRAM · A PYRAMID OF ENERGY

Always widest at the base

1 · producer1,0002 · primary consumer1003 · secondary consumer104 · tertiary consumer1energy in each level

Bars are not drawn to scale. Under the 10% rule of thumb, each bar would be a tenth as wide as the one below it. Real efficiencies vary from one ecosystem to another. The pink dots are energy leaving as heat.

WHAT IT TELLS YOU

Three things to remember

GREATEST AT THE BASEThe primary producers always hold the most energy. A higher level never has more production than the level below it.
ABOUT 10% MOVES UPOn average only about 10% of the energy in one trophic level is transferred to the next.
AN EXAMPLE1,000 units in grass, 100 in the lemmings that eat it, 10 in the foxes, 1 in the eagle.
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Use the rule of thumb

Producers make 50,000 units of energy. With no other information, how much production do you expect at the secondary consumer level?

Two steps up, 10% each time: 50,000 × 0.10 = 5,000 for primary consumers, then 5,000 × 0.10 = 500.

Only about a tenth moves up. Here is where the rest goes.
STEP 8 · WHY SO LITTLE MOVES UP

Trophic efficiency: where the energy goes

Trophic efficiency is the amount of energy at one trophic level divided by the amount at the level below it. It is small because, at three separate points, energy fails to reach the next level.

INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW 1,000 UNITS OF ENERGY

Three filters between a plant and a herbivore

Tap the buttons, or Next filter, to click through all 4
plants made
1,000eaten
500eaten
500eaten
500not eaten
500not eaten
500not eaten
500DETRITUSDETRITUSDETRITUSassimilated
250assimilated
250feces 250feces 250new biomass
100respired 150
leaves as heat
START · WHAT THE PLANTS MADE1,000 units of energy in plant tissueThis is the net primary production: the energy stored in the plants that a herbivore could, in principle, eat. Follow it to see how much becomes herbivore.
FILTER 1 · CONSUMPTION EFFICIENCYNot everything gets eatenConsumption efficiency (CE) is the fraction of production at one trophic level that is consumed by the next. Here the herbivores eat 500 of the 1,000: CE = 500 ÷ 1,000 = 50%.The rest is never eaten. It dies and becomes detritus.
FILTER 2 · ASSIMILATION EFFICIENCYNot everything eaten is digestedAssimilation efficiency (AE) is the fraction of the food consumed that is assimilated. A lot of what is eaten cannot be digested and leaves as feces.Here 250 of the 500 is assimilated: AE = 250 ÷ 500 = 50%.
FILTER 3 · PRODUCTION EFFICIENCYMost of what is digested gets burnedProduction efficiency (PE) is the fraction of the assimilated food that is turned into new consumer biomass. Most of it is used to make ATP and power the body, and leaves as heat.Here 100 of the 250 becomes new tissue: PE = 100 ÷ 250 = 40%.Trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE = 0.50 × 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.10. That is the 10%.

A worked example with round numbers that land on the 10% average. Real values differ from one ecosystem to another.

THE CALCULATION

Multiply the three together

trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE
production at the next level = production at this level × CE × AE × PE
IF YOU ARE GIVEN CE, AE AND PEMultiply them, then multiply by the production you started with.
IF YOU ARE NOTUse the rule of thumb: about 10% per level.
CHECK YOURSELF · TAP TO OPEN

Work one through

A groundhog has 10,000 g of plant biomass available. Consumption efficiency is 20%, assimilation efficiency is 50% and production efficiency is 20%. How much biomass does it gain?

10,000 × 0.20 × 0.50 × 0.20 = 200 g. Step by step: 2,000 g eaten, 1,000 g assimilated, 200 g turned into new groundhog.

HOW MUCH REALLY GETS EATEN

Consumption efficiency in the real world

On land · about 13% of primary production is consumed
In water · about 35%

On average, most of what plants make is never eaten at all.

DIAGRAM · DIGESTION IS HARD WORK

Why production efficiency is so low

has not eaten recentlyhas just eatenheartgut hard at work

A python that has just eaten is working far harder than one that has not: its heart and gut are running at full tilt just to deal with the meal. All of that work is paid for with energy from the food, and it leaves as heat. Only what is left over can become new snake.

DATA · WHAT THIS MEANS FOR FOOD

An extra trophic level is expensive

Share of farmland used for livestock · 83%
Share of our food calories that livestock provide · 18%
Share of our protein · 37%

Animals raised for food are one trophic level above the crops they eat, so most of the energy in those crops never reaches our plates.

Figures from Poore and Nemecek, Science.

Energy sets the limits. Within them, some species matter far more than others.
STEP 9 · NOT EVERY SPECIES MATTERS EQUALLY

Keystone, dominant and engineer

Three labels for species that shape their whole community. They are easy to mix up, so start with the picture that separates the first two, then open each one.

GRAPH · IMPACT VS. HOW MUCH OF IT THERE IS

The difference in one picture

↑ TOTAL IMPACT OF THE SPECIES
KEYSTONEsmall biomass, big impactDOMINANTbig biomass, big impactmost species
PROPORTIONAL BIOMASS OF THE SPECIES →

A dominant species matters because there is so much of it. A keystone species matters far more than its amount would suggest. An ecosystem engineer is defined differently: by what it does to the habitat.

3 EXAMPLES · TAP A CARD TO SWITCH BETWEEN THEM
1

What it is

A species whose effect on its community is out of proportion to its abundance or biomass. Most of that effect is indirect.

HOW TO SPOT ONEThere is not much of it, yet removing it changes which other species can live there.
THE TESTTake it away. If the community is reshaped far more than its small numbers would suggest, it is a keystone.
2

Examples, as a chart

CHART · HOW MUCH THERE IS VS. HOW MUCH IT MATTERS
The seastar Pisaster
SHARE OF BIOMASS
IMPACT
It eats mussels. Without it, mussels crowd out almost everything else on the rock. Step 10 is the experiment.
Sea otters
SHARE OF BIOMASS
IMPACT
They eat sea urchins. Without otters, urchins graze the kelp forest away.

Bars show the pattern, small share and large impact. They are not measured values.

↑ Back to the 3 example cards
1

What it is

A species that is very common, and has a large effect on the community because there is so much of it.

HOW TO SPOT ONEIt makes up a large share of the community's biomass.
NOT THE SAME AS KEYSTONEIts impact is large, but it is in proportion to its amount. Maple trees are dominant. They are not a keystone species.
2

Examples, as a chart

CHART · HOW MUCH THERE IS VS. HOW MUCH IT MATTERS
Maple trees
SHARE OF BIOMASS
IMPACT
The dominant trees in many eastern North American temperate forests.
Mussels
SHARE OF BIOMASS
IMPACT
They dominate the rocky intertidal, which is exactly why the seastar that eats them matters so much.

Bars show the pattern, large share and large impact. They are not measured values.

↑ Back to the 3 example cards
1

What it is

An organism that creates, maintains, destroys or otherwise substantially alters a habitat.

HOW TO SPOT ONEThe physical place is different because the organism is there.
WHY WOLVES ARE NOT ONEWolves change Yellowstone through who they eat. They do not physically rebuild the habitat. Beavers do.
2

Example, before and after

BEFORE BEAVERSA narrow stream through the trees.
AFTER BEAVERSA dam, a pond, a lodge, and felled trees.

The dam turns a stream into a pond. Everything that lives there now lives in a habitat the beaver built.

↑ Back to the 3 example cards
Here is the experiment that showed what a keystone species is.
STEP 10 · REAL-LIFE EXAMPLE

The seastar that held a shoreline together

The classic keystone experiment. One predator, removed from one stretch of rocky shore, for more than ten years.

1

The setup

On the rocky intertidal of the Pacific coast, mussels dominate. The seastar Pisaster eats a range of invertebrates, especially mussels, and sets the lower limit of where mussels can live.

MUSSELSThe dominant species. Left alone, they take over the rock.
PISASTERA predator. Far less of it than there is of mussels.
2

The experiment

Seastars were removed from an experimental site and kept out. A matching site was left alone as the control.

CONTROL · SEASTARS PRESENTMany kinds of organism share the rock.
SEASTARS REMOVEDMussels take over the rock.
3

The result

↑ NUMBER OF SPECIES PRESENT
5101520’63’66’68’71’73seastars presentseastars removed
YEAR →

With seastars, the number of species stayed high. Without them it collapsed within about three years and never recovered.

Points are read from the published graph, so treat the exact values as approximate.

4

Why

No seastarsmussels spreadno room for othersspecies lost

The seastar never touched most of those lost species. By eating mussels it kept space open for them. That is an indirect effect.

WHAT THIS EXAMPLE TEACHES

A keystone species

Pisaster is a small part of the community by biomass, yet removing it changed which species could live there. Its impact is out of proportion to its abundance.

A predator is not the only thing that can remove a species.
STEP 11 · ONE MORE PLAYER

Parasites shape food webs too

Parasites rarely appear in food web drawings, but they can change a community as much as a predator can.

INTERACTIVE · A DISEASE REMOVES A KEYSTONE SPECIES

Missing from the picture, not from the web

producerherbivorepredatorparasitesdecomposersboth touch every level, and both are usually left off the drawing
HOW A PARASITE REACHES A WHOLE COMMUNITY

Through its host

Parasitehost does worseeverything the host affects changes

A parasite lowers the fitness of its host. If that host is a keystone species or a top predator, the effects spread through the web by the same indirect routes you saw in Steps 4 to 10.

TRY THIS ONE

Sea star wasting syndrome

A disease is killing seastars along the coast. Based on Step 10, what should happen to the rest of the community?

Losing seastars to disease is like the removal experiment, run by a disease. With fewer seastars, mussels should spread, crowd the rock, and the number of species should fall.
