Module 2.3 · Energy, Matter & Trophic Levels →

Lock it in · Part 2

  1. Autotrophs make their own food. Heterotrophs get it from other organisms. Photo- means light, chemo- means chemical.
  2. Food web arrows point from the food to the eater, the direction the energy moves.
  3. Count the levels below an organism to name it. One that eats from two or more levels is a trophic omnivore.
  4. Direct effects are between species that interact. Indirect effects pass through a species in between.
  5. A trophic cascade starts with a top predator and reaches every level below, flipping direction each time.
  6. A pyramid of energy is always widest at the base. About 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next.
  7. Trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE: the fraction eaten, times the fraction assimilated, times the fraction turned into new biomass.
  8. Keystone: impact out of proportion to its biomass. Dominant: big impact because there is so much of it. Engineer: it changes the habitat.
  9. Parasites and decomposers are left off most food webs, but a disease that removes a keystone species reshapes the whole community.
THE WHOLE MODULE IN ONE LINE Two engulfing events gave eukaryotes mitochondria and chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are why plants and algae can capture light energy, and food webs trace where that energy goes, from species to species.

Notes

Everything you are expected to know for this module, in the order the learning objectives ask for it. Read it once, then use the checklist at the end.

IN THESE NOTES1 · Two kinds of cell2 · The theory of endosymbiosis3 · Five lines of evidence4 · Where the genes went5 · Reading a food web6 · Direct and indirect effects7 · Trophic cascades8 · Keystone, dominant, engineer9 · Parasites10 · Energy up the web11 · Exam checklist
THE BIG IDEA

Two engulfing events gave eukaryotes their mitochondria and chloroplasts. Chloroplasts are why plants and algae can capture light energy. A food web traces where that energy goes, and because everything in a web is connected, changing one species can change species it never touches.

SECTION 1

Background: bacterial vs. eukaryotic cells

BACTERIAL CELLEUKARYOTIC CELL
NucleusNoneYes
Mitochondria, chloroplastsNoneMitochondria in all. Chloroplasts in photosynthetic ones.
DNAMost of it is a single circular chromosomeChromosomes in the nucleus
Cell divisionBinary fissionMitosis and meiosis
WHY THIS COMES FIRSTCircular DNA and binary fission are bacterial traits. Finding them inside a eukaryotic cell is the heart of the evidence below.

Three domains

  • Every living thing is in one of three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes.
  • Mitochondria and chloroplasts are found only in eukaryotes. No bacterium and no archaeon has them. That is the puzzle the theory solves.

Binary fission, in order

  • 1. The one circular chromosome is attached to the inside of the cell membrane.
  • 2. DNA replication starts at one spot, the origin of replication, and runs both ways around the circle.
  • 3. Now there are two circles, each attached to the membrane at its own site.
  • 4. The cell grows longer and the two sites move apart.
  • 5. At about twice its first size, the cell pinches in at the middle.
  • 6. New membrane and wall form there. Two daughter cells, each with the same DNA as the parent.
SECTION 2

The theory of endosymbiosis

  • Symbiosis: a close interaction between species that has evolved over a long time. Endosymbiosis: a symbiosis in which one species lives inside the other.
  • Mitochondria were once free-living alpha-proteobacteria. They were engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell and became obligate mutualists.
  • Chloroplasts were once free-living cyanobacteria. They were engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell that already had mitochondria.
  • Lynn Margulis championed the theory. The DNA evidence was conclusive.
  • On the tree of life: both organelles arose from bacteria, not from archaea and not from other eukaryotes. Event 1 (mitochondria) happened at the base of the eukaryote branch. Event 2 (chloroplasts) happened later, in one lineage.
  • All eukaryotes have mitochondria. All photosynthetic eukaryotes have chloroplasts.
  • Not all photosynthetic eukaryotes are plants. Many are algae on other branches, such as diatoms, brown algae and dinoflagellates.
  • The host most likely engulfed the bacterium as prey, but did not digest it. Over evolutionary time it became essential to the host.
MITOCHONDRIONCellular respiration. Makes most of the ATP that powers the cell. From an alpha-proteobacterium.
CHLOROPLASTPhotosynthesis. Converts light energy into chemical energy. From a cyanobacterium.
WHICH CAME FIRST?Mitochondria. How you know: all eukaryotes have mitochondria, but only photosynthetic ones have chloroplasts as well. The cyanobacterium was engulfed by a cell that already had mitochondria.
  • Who was shaped by endosymbiosis? Every eukaryote, through mitochondria. Plants and algae twice, through chloroplasts as well.
  • Photosynthetic but not plants: algae, and cyanobacteria. Cyanobacteria are bacteria, not plants.

The cast

ALPHA-PROTEOBACTERIUMFree-living. One branch of the proteobacteria, the most diverse group of bacteria. Takes in organic molecules and O₂ and gets energy by aerobic respiration. Becomes the mitochondrion.
CYANOBACTERIUMFree-living. The one group of bacteria that photosynthesizes as plants do: light and water in, oxygen out. Light reactions on internal membranes. Becomes the chloroplast.
THE HOSTAn ancestral eukaryotic cell, much larger, able to wrap its membrane around a particle and take it in. Whether it already had a nucleus is not resolved.
  • A cyanobacterium is not a chloroplast. It is a whole free-living bacterium, and its relatives are still alive today.
  • Symbiont: an organism in a closely evolved association with another species. Endosymbiont: the one living inside. The cell it lives in is the host.

Where the events sit on the tree

  • Event 1, about 2 billion years ago, joins the stem of the eukaryotes before today's groups split. So every eukaryote inherited mitochondria.
  • Event 2 joins one branch only: the common ancestor of the red algae and green algae. Land plants arose later from the green algae and carry the same chloroplasts, wrapped in two membranes. This is primary endosymbiosis.
  • Nothing jumped between domains. One bacterium was engulfed and kept dividing inside its host. Each time the host divided, its daughters got some. Its free-living relatives are still bacteria.
  • Today the host supplies protection and resources, and the organelle supplies energy the host can use.

Who had the idea

  • Konstantin Merezhkovsky, early 1900s: chloroplasts look like cyanobacteria, and corals keep algae as symbionts. It could not be tested then.
  • Lynn Margulis, 1967: brought it back with new data from cell and molecular biology, including electron micrographs of chloroplasts.
  • DNA sequencing was the decisive test.

Chloroplasts on many branches

  • Paulinella chromatophora, a photosynthetic amoeba, took in a cyanobacterium from a different branch, separately and more recently. Its chloroplast still holds about one-third to one-half of the ancestral genome, so the change to organelle is still in progress.
  • Chloroplasts turn up on many eukaryote branches: diatoms, brown algae, dinoflagellates and euglenids all photosynthesize and none is a plant. Apicomplexans keep a leftover chloroplast but no longer photosynthesize.
SECTION 3KNOW ALL FIVE

The evidence: five lines

EVIDENCEWHAT WE FINDWHY IT POINTS TO BACTERIA
1 · SizeMitochondria are the size of alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplasts are the size of cyanobacteria.A former bacterium should be bacterium-sized.
2 · Own genomeEach organelle has its own genome, organized as a circular DNA molecule.That is how bacteria package DNA.
3 · DivisionBoth divide by binary fission.Bacteria divide this way. Eukaryotic cells divide by mitosis and meiosis.
4 · MembranesBoth have two (or more) membranes.Consistent with being engulfed.
5 · DNA sequencesMitochondrial DNA nests with the alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplast DNA nests with the cyanobacteria.It shows descent, and names the exact groups.
THE MOST CONVINCINGNumber 5, the DNA sequences. The first four show that the organelles resemble bacteria. The molecular phylogenies show which bacteria they descended from.
  • The logic: nobody watched it happen. If the organelles were once bacteria, they should still look, divide and test like bacteria today. Each clue is a prediction that checks out.
  • Membranes, the standard picture: the host's membrane folds around the bacterium and becomes the outer membrane. The bacterium's own membrane becomes the inner one. The real history is messier, so remember the number: two or more.
  • Electron microscope: the parallel photosynthetic membranes of a cyanobacterium show up inside red algal and plant chloroplasts. A fine resemblance, but it did not settle the question.
  • The DNA test uses the gene for small ribosomal RNA, which every cell has. The organelle's copy matches a free-living bacterium far above chance and its own cell's nucleus only a little above chance. Family trees built from many species place mitochondria among the alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplasts among the cyanobacteria.
SECTION 4

Where the genes went

  • Free-living cyanobacteria and alpha-proteobacteria have thousands of genes. Chloroplasts and mitochondria have dozens.
  • Some genes migrated to the nucleus of the host. Others were lost, because they were not needed inside a cell.
  • A few eukaryotes have no mitochondria. They most likely lost them, and they still carry mitochondrial genes in the nuclear genome. So mitochondria still count as a universal feature of eukaryotes: every eukaryote descends from a cell that had them.
  • How and when the nucleus first originated is not resolved. It is an active area of research.
CYANOBACTERIA2,000 to 3,000 genes.
CHLOROPLASTS60 to 200 genes.
HUMAN MITOCHONDRIAGenes for just 13 proteins and 24 RNAs.
  • Three fates for the missing genes. Lost, because a nuclear gene already did the job. Moved to the nucleus when an organelle broke open and spilled its DNA. Moved on a virus.
  • Many moved genes still serve the organelle. The nucleus of the plant Arabidopsis holds several thousand genes of cyanobacterial origin, and some make proteins that are sent back into the chloroplast.

Eukaryotes with no mitochondria

  • First idea: they branched off before mitochondria existed. Abandoned, because their nuclei carry genes from the mitochondrial symbiont.
  • Hydrogenosome: a highly altered mitochondrion that makes ATP without oxygen, with little or no DNA.
  • Mitosome: smaller still. It makes no ATP but keeps genes for building iron-sulfur clusters.

Where the evidence runs out

  • A eukaryote's nucleus mixes genes from four sources: the symbionts, other bacteria (horizontal gene transfer), genes found only in eukaryotes, and genes related to archaea, including those for transcription and translation.
  • Asgard archaea: first pieced together in 2015 from Arctic sea-floor hot springs, with genes like those that organize a eukaryotic cell. More than 600 kinds were known by 2021. The host cell most likely descended from archaea like these.
  • Two hypotheses. Nucleus first: the host was already a eukaryote when it engulfed the bacterium. Symbiosis first: an archaeon and a proteobacterium joined, and the nucleus came later. A problem for the first: no eukaryote has ever been found that never had mitochondria.
SECTION 5

Reading a food chain and a food web

AUTO- · SELFAn autotroph makes its own food.
HETERO- · OTHERA heterotroph gets its food from other organisms.
PHOTO- · LIGHTEnergy from light.
CHEMO- · CHEMICALEnergy from chemicals.
THE ARROW RULEArrows show the flow of energy. They go from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it. Grass → elk → wolf. Drawing them the other way round is the classic mistake.
WHAT IS BELOW ITNAMETROPHIC LEVEL
Nothing. It makes its own food.Primary producer1
ProducersPrimary consumer2
Primary consumersSecondary consumer3
Secondary consumersTertiary consumer4
Two or more levelsTrophic omnivoreNo single level
  • A food chain is one path through a food web: one producer, then what eats it, then what eats that. A web holds many chains.
  • Trophic omnivore: an organism that feeds on two or more trophic levels. Anything that feeds on a trophic omnivore is classed as one too.
  • Often missing from the drawing: decomposers (bacteria, archaea, fungi) and parasites.
COMMON MIX-UPIn everyday use an omnivore eats plants and animals. In ecology a trophic omnivore is defined by trophic levels. A consumer that eats primary and secondary consumers is one, even if it never eats a plant.
SECTION 6

Direct and indirect effects

DIRECT EFFECTBetween two species that interact with each other. One eats the other, for example.
INDIRECT EFFECTBetween two species that do not interact directly. It passes through one or more species in between.
  • The test: is there a species in the middle? If yes, it is indirect.
  • Sign trick: two negatives in a row make a positive. Wolves lower elk, elk lower willows, so wolves help willows.
  • Moose in Yellowstone: willows and aspen affect them directly (food). Wolves affect them directly (predator). Elk and beaver affect them indirectly, by eating the same plants.
SECTION 7

Trophic cascades

A trophic cascade is when a top predator influences the density of species at every trophic level below it. It is a chain of indirect effects that starts at the top.

WOLVESELKWILLOWS AND ASPEN
Without wolvesGoneUpDown
With wolves backUpDownUp
  • Three checks: it starts at the top, it reaches every level below, and the direction flips at each level.
  • A change that starts with a producer or a primary consumer is not a trophic cascade.
  • It is a top-down effect: the change starts with the top predator and travels down the web.
  • Behavior counts too. With wolves around, elk spend less time feeding where they are easy to catch. Less browsing there lets willows and aspen recover, so primary production goes up in those places.
  • The wolves of Yellowstone, as the story is told: wolves return, elk avoid the valleys, willow and aspen regrow, songbirds and beavers move in, beaver ponds make homes for more species, and the regrown vegetation holds the banks, so there is less erosion and the rivers steady. How much of this is down to the wolves is debated.
  • Cascade diagram vs. food web: a food web shows who eats whom. A cascade diagram shows how abundance changes level by level.
  • Omnivory complicates it. If the web has trophic omnivores, you cannot predict the effect of removing a consumer without data on how strong the direct and indirect effects are.
SECTION 8

Keystone species, dominant species, ecosystem engineers

TYPEDEFINITIONEXAMPLE
Keystone speciesIts effect on the community is out of proportion to its abundance or biomass.The seastar Pisaster. Sea otters.
Dominant speciesVery common, and has a large effect because there is so much of it.Maple trees in eastern North American forests. Mussels on the rocky shore.
Ecosystem engineerIt creates, maintains, destroys or substantially alters a habitat.Beavers.
WHY BEAVERS BUT NOT WOLVESWolves change Yellowstone through who they eat. They do not physically rebuild the habitat. Beavers do: a dam turns a stream into a pond.
EXPERIMENT TO KNOW · PISASTERSetup: on the rocky intertidal, seastars were removed from an experimental site and kept out. A site with seastars was the control. Result: with seastars, the number of species stayed high. Without them, mussels took over the rock and the number of species fell sharply. Conclusion: Pisaster is a keystone species. By eating mussels it keeps space open for species it never touches, which is an indirect effect.
SECTION 9

Parasites in food webs

  • A parasite lowers the fitness of its host. That changes every species the host affects.
  • If the host is a keystone species or a top predator, the effect spreads through the whole web.
  • Example: sea star wasting syndrome removes seastars, like the removal experiment run by a disease. Expect mussels to spread and the number of species to fall.
  • Not everything that feeds is a predator or parasite. A tree shrew feeds on a pitcher plant's nectar and leaves droppings in the pitcher. The shrew gets food, the plant gets nitrogen: a mutualism. The pitcher plant is still a primary producer.
  • Parasites and decomposers are both usually left off food web drawings, although both are always there.
SECTION 10STEPS 7 AND 8

Trophic pyramids and trophic efficiency

  • A trophic pyramid shows the energy in each trophic level. Energy is highest at the base, in the primary producers. A higher level never has more production than the level below it.
  • Digestion is hard work. A python that has just eaten runs its heart and gut far harder than a fasting one. That energy leaves as heat, which is part of why production efficiency is low.
  • On average only about 10% of the energy in one level is transferred to the next. That is what limits the number of trophic levels.
  • The amount at each level can be given as mass (kg of carbon) or as energy (kilocalories). A kilogram of carbon is not itself a unit of energy: it measures organic matter, and the energy is stored in that matter, so one can stand for the other.
EFFICIENCYTHE QUESTION IT ANSWERSTO KNOW
Consumption · CEHow much of the available food is actually eaten?On average 13% of primary production on land, 35% in water.
Assimilation · AEHow much of what is eaten is digested?The rest leaves as waste in feces.
Production · PEHow much of what is digested builds new biomass?Most goes to making ATP by cellular respiration instead.
trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE
production at the next level = production at this level × trophic efficiency
TWO KINDS OF QUESTIONGiven CE, AE and PE: multiply them, then multiply by the lower level's production. Example: 0.50 × 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.10, so 1,000 units below gives 100 above. Not given them: use the rule of thumb, 10%.
REAL WORLDMore than 80% of farmland is used for livestock, yet that supplies just 18% of our food calories and 37% of our protein. Livestock are primary consumers, so only about 10% of the energy in their feed becomes animal biomass.
SECTION 11

Exam checklist

You're ready when you can:

  • Put the six steps of binary fission in order, starting with DNA replication.
  • Name the two free-living bacteria and the host, and say which became which organelle.
  • Place Event 1 and Event 2 on the tree of life, and explain why nothing jumped between domains.
  • Explain the evidence for endosymbiosis, and say which line is the most convincing and why.
  • Give the three fates of the missing genes, and explain hydrogenosomes and mitosomes.
  • Say what the Asgard archaea suggest, and state the two hypotheses for the origin of the eukaryotic cell.
  • Explain what food web arrows represent and why they run from the organism eaten to the eater.
  • Find the primary producers, primary and secondary consumers and trophic omnivores in any food web, and trace a food chain inside it.
  • Say what a trophic pyramid represents.
  • Explain how interactions among species create indirect effects.
  • Tell keystone species, dominant species and ecosystem engineers apart, with an example of each.
  • Explain how a keystone species changes community structure, using the Pisaster experiment.
  • Explain how a trophic cascade changes community composition, and what makes something a cascade.
  • Explain why omnivory makes the effect of removing a consumer hard to predict.
  • Explain how parasites can change community structure.
  • Explain how CE, AE and PE combine into trophic efficiency, and calculate production at a higher level with them or with the 10% rule.
COMMON MIX-UPKeystone is not the same as important or common. A dominant species matters because of how much of it there is. A keystone species matters far more than its amount would suggest.
COMMON MIX-UPNot every chain of effects is a trophic cascade. It has to start with a top predator and reach every level below.

Infographics

Every diagram from the flow charts in one place, without the reading in between. Start with the one-page map, then scan the rest.

INFOGRAPHIC 1 · THE WHOLE MODULE ON ONE PAGE
PART 1

Endosymbiosis

The mitochondria powering your cells were once free-living bacteria. How do we know?

1A bacterial cell: what it has and what it lacks
The theory is about bacteria that ended up living inside other cells. So start with the bacterium itself.
2Binary fission
When bacterial cells divide, they do it by binary fission : the cell copies its DNA, grows, and splits in two. Eukaryotic cells divide by different processes, mitosis and meiosis. 1 , 2
3Two free-living bacteria, and the cell that engulfed them
Before any of this happened there were no mitochondria and no chloroplasts anywhere. There were bacteria living on their own, and there was a larger cell that could swallow things. Meet the two bacteria first, as they were: free.
4Two events on the tree of life
Endosymbiosis has been fundamentally important to the origin of eukaryotes.
5One cell living inside another
Symbiosis is a close interaction between species that has evolved over a long time. Endosymbiosis is a symbiosis in which one species lives inside the other. 1 , 2
6Two engulfing events, in order
The host did not start out with mitochondria or chloroplasts. It gained them one at a time, by engulfing a bacterium and keeping it. 2
7From those two events to you and to plants
Follow the host cell forward. One branch of its descendants stopped after Event 1. Another went through Event 2 as well. 2
8What to notice in each one
Both still carry clear signs of where they came from: their own DNA and more than one membrane. 2
9Testing the theory: five predictions
Nobody watched any of this happen. So the theory is tested the way any claim about the past is tested: if it is true, what should we still be able to see today? 2
10Where did the genes go?
Engulfing a bacterium was only the beginning. Chloroplasts and mitochondria have far fewer genes than the free-living bacteria they came from: thousands of genes became dozens. So where did the rest of each genome go? 1 , 2
11Eukaryotes with no mitochondria
Most eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria, but a few single-celled eukaryotes that live in oxygen-free environments do not. Does that break the rule that all eukaryotes have them? Biologists had two ways to explain these cells. 1
12Still open: the origin of the eukaryotic cell itself
If mitochondria began as proteobacteria and chloroplasts as cyanobacteria, where did the rest of the eukaryotic cell come from? This is where settled science ends and active research begins. 1
13Where this part comes from
The small numbers in the text point to this list.
PART 2

Food webs

Some organisms make their own food and the rest get theirs from other organisms. So who eats whom, and what happens to everyone else when one species disappears?

1Two ways to get food
Part 1 ended with two kinds of eukaryotic cell: one with chloroplasts and one without. Among eukaryotes, that difference goes with two ways of getting food.
2A food chain, and what the arrows mean
Line up who eats whom and you get a food chain. Each position has a name.
3A food web: many chains at once
No community is one neat chain. Most organisms eat more than one thing and are eaten by more than one thing. Draw all of it and you have a food web .
4Direct and indirect effects
Because everything in a web is connected, a change in one species reaches others it never touches.
5Trophic cascades
When a top predator influences the density of species at every trophic level below it, that is a trophic cascade . It is a chain of indirect effects that starts at the top.
6The tree shrew and the pitcher plant
A tree shrew sits on a pitcher plant, feeds on the nectar it makes, and leaves its droppings in the pitcher. Two questions: at what trophic level is the plant, and what kind of interaction is this?
7Trophic pyramids: pyramids of energy
Stack the trophic levels and make each bar as wide as the energy that level holds. The result always has the same shape.
8Trophic efficiency: where the energy goes
Trophic efficiency is the amount of energy at one trophic level divided by the amount at the level below it. It is small because, at three separate points, energy fails to reach the next level.
9Keystone, dominant and engineer
Three labels for species that shape their whole community. They are easy to mix up, so start with the picture that separates the first two, then open each one.
10The seastar that held a shoreline together
The classic keystone experiment. One predator, removed from one stretch of rocky shore, for more than ten years.
11Parasites shape food webs too
Parasites rarely appear in food web drawings, but they can change a community as much as a predator can.

WHAT A BACTERIAL CELL HASSmall and simple, but a complete living thing
A CELL MEMBRANE AND A CELL WALLThe membrane encloses the cell. The wall sits outside it and holds the cell's shape.

WHERE THE ENERGY WORK HAPPENSOn the membrane and in the cytoplasmA bacterium has no mitochondria, yet it still has to get energy out of food. That work is done by proteins floating in the cytoplasm or embedded in the cell membrane.A few bacteria, notably the photosynthetic ones, also have internal membranes, and their light reactions happen there.In a eukaryotic cell the same two jobs happen inside organelles: aerobic respiration in the mitochondrion, photosynthesis in the chloroplast.

2 · Binary fission
INFOGRAPHIC 3
INTERACTIVE · SIX FRAMES

Watch one cell become two

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
attached to the membraneone circle of DNAcopying starts at one spotand runs both ways roundtwo attachment sitestwo circles of DNAthe sites move apartthe cell gets longerpinches in at the middleabout twice its first sizetwo daughter cellssame DNA in each
1 · BEFORE DIVIDINGOne circular DNA molecule, attached to the membraneThe cell's circular chromosome is held against the inside of the cell membrane by proteins (the pink dot).
2 · COPY THE DNAReplication starts at one spot and runs both waysBinary fission begins with DNA replication. Copying starts at a specific location, the origin of replication, and proceeds in opposite directions around the circle.
3 · TWO CIRCLESEach copy gets its own attachment siteThe result is two DNA molecules, each attached to the membrane at a different site. At first the two sites are close together.
4 · GROWThe cell lengthens and the copies move apartAs the cell elongates, the two attachment sites are carried away from each other, and each takes its DNA circle with it.
5 · PINCHA constriction forms at the midpointWhen the cell is about twice its original size and the two DNA molecules are well separated, the cell pinches in at the middle.
6 · TWO CELLSNew membrane and wall finish the jobNew cell membrane and cell wall are built at the constriction, dividing the one cell into two.Each daughter cell has the same genetic material as the parent cell.

4 · Two events on the tree of life

INTERACTIVE · THE TREE OF LIFE, AND TWO LINEAGES THAT MOVED IN

Where mitochondria and chloroplasts came from

rootBACTERIAEUKARYOTESalpha-proteobacteriacyanobacteriaother bacteriaARCHAEAother eukaryotesplants + other

THE TREE OF LIFEThree domains, and one of them is oursEvery living thing belongs to one of three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes. Read the tree from the root to the tips: time runs that way, and every tip is alive today.Animals and plants are twigs on a single branch, the eukaryotes (boxed). Mitochondria and chloroplasts are found only on that branch.
EVENT 1 · GAVE RISE TO MITOCHONDRIAA line of bacteria joins the stem of the eukaryotesFollow the amber line. It leaves the alpha-proteobacteria branch and meets the eukaryote stem at the flashing dot. That meeting is the engulfing, about 2 billion years ago.2The dot sits on the stem before the point where today's eukaryote groups split apart. So the amber line then runs up every one of those branches: all eukaryotes inherited mitochondria.
EVENT 2 · GAVE RISE TO CHLOROPLASTSA second line of bacteria joins one eukaryote branchFollow the green line. It leaves the cyanobacteria branch and meets just one eukaryote branch, the one leading to plants and other photosynthetic eukaryotes.It joins after the split, so only that branch carries it. Animals and fungi are on other branches and never had chloroplasts. The cell it joined already carried the amber line, so mitochondria came first.
WHAT THE LINES MEANNothing jumped. A lineage moved in and has been inherited ever sinceA bacterium did not turn into a eukaryote, and it did not hop from one domain to another. One bacterium was taken inside a host cell and kept dividing there. Each time the host cell divided, its daughter cells received some of them. That has continued, without a break, to this day.So every mitochondrion in you is a direct descendant of that one engulfed bacterium. The two white rings mark the common ancestors: from there, one line stayed free-living and leads to today's bacteria, and the other went inside and leads to today's organelles. They are relatives.Each event belongs to a branch, at one point along it. Everything that descends from that point inherited the organelle. Event 1 sits below the branching point of the living eukaryotes, Event 2 above it.
TAP THE FOUR BUTTONS IN ORDERWhere on the tree did the two organelles come from?The amber and green lines are lines of descent, like every other branch on the tree. Watch where each one comes from, where it joins, and where it goes afterwards.

INFOGRAPHIC 10
WHO HAD THE IDEA

An old idea that had to wait for its evidence

early 1900s1967DNA sequencingthe ideanew evidencethe decisive test
1Konstantin Merezhkovsky, more than a century ago
He saw that chloroplasts closely resemble cyanobacteria, and he knew that corals keep algae inside their tissues as symbionts. He put the two together: chloroplasts began as symbiotic cyanobacteria. With the tools of the time it could not be tested, and it was set aside, more neglected than disproved.1
2Lynn Margulis, 1967
She brought the idea back and supported it with new kinds of data from cell and molecular biology, including what the electron microscope showed inside chloroplasts.
3Then DNA could be read
Chloroplasts and mitochondria turned out to have DNA of their own. Comparing its sequence with bacterial DNA was the decisive test. Step 9 lets you do both checks yourself.
6 · Two engulfing events, in order
INFOGRAPHIC 11
EVENT 1 · ABOUT 2 BILLION YEARS AGO

The alpha-proteobacterium moves in

1The host, an ancestral eukaryotic cell with no mitochondria, meets a free-living alpha-proteobacterium.
2The host engulfs it, most likely as prey: a predator swallowing its food.
3It is not digested. It survives inside the host.
4Over a very long time it becomes the mitochondrion.
INFOGRAPHIC 12
EVENT 2 · LATER

The cyanobacterium moves in

1A descendant of that cell, which already has mitochondria, meets a free-living cyanobacterium.
2The host engulfs it.
3It survives inside the host too.
4Over a very long time it becomes the chloroplast.

STRAIGHT OUT OF EVENT 2

Red algae, green algae, and then land plants

common ancestorafter Event 2red algaegreen algaeland plants

The engulfing of a cyanobacterium happened in a common ancestor of the green algae and the red algae. Both groups inherited its chloroplasts. Land plants arose later, from among the green algae, and carry the same chloroplasts.1

Their chloroplasts are wrapped in two membranes, which is what an engulfed cyanobacterium would leave behind.

ROUTE 1 · LOSTSome genes were simply no longer neededA free-living bacterium has to make everything for itself. Inside a host cell it does not. If a similar gene in the nucleus could already supply what the chloroplast required, the chloroplast's own copy could be lost with no harm done.So these genes were not mislaid. Living inside another cell made them unnecessary, and over time they disappeared. The textbook is careful here: it says some genes may simply have been lost this way.1
ROUTE 2 · MOVED WHEN AN ORGANELLE BROKEDNA spilled out and ended up in the nucleusWhen a chloroplast broke open, its DNA was released inside the host cell, and some of it ended up in the nucleus.Many genes were transported to the nucleus this way.
ROUTE 3 · MOVED ON A VIRUSSome genes hitched a rideViruses carry genetic material from place to place. Some chloroplast genes reached the nucleus by hitching a ride with them.The textbook names this as a second route to the nucleus, alongside Route 2. It is not the only way genes moved, and the textbook gives no further detail on it.
AFTER THE MOVEMany of the moved genes still serve the organelleThe nuclear genome of the flowering plant Arabidopsis contains several thousand genes of cyanobacterial origin. Some of them code for proteins that are made by the host cell and then used inside the chloroplast.1So the chloroplast now depends on genes it no longer carries. Mitochondria tell the same story: many genes from the original bacterial endosymbiont migrated to the nucleus, where they still reside.

Drawn for a chloroplast. A simplified picture: one chloroplast and a few genes stand in for many.

THE FIRST HYPOTHESISThey branched off before mitochondria existedBiologists originally thought these eukaryotes were leftovers from a time before Event 1: cells with a nucleus that had never taken in the bacterium.That proposal was abandoned. These cells turned out to have genes in their nucleus that migrated there from the mitochondrial symbiont. A cell that never had the symbiont could not have its genes.
THE SUPPORTED HYPOTHESISThey had mitochondria once, and lost themThe textbook reports that every mitochondria-free eukaryote examined has relict mitochondrial genes in its nuclear genome (the amber dots).1So their ancestors went through Event 1 like every other eukaryote. These organisms live in oxygen-free environments, and over time their mitochondria were lost or, as the next drawing shows, altered to suit life without oxygen.
INFOGRAPHIC 27
INTERACTIVE · WHAT IS LEFT OF THE MITOCHONDRION

From mitochondrion to remnant

Tap the buttons, or Next organelle, to click through all 3
genes of
mitochondrial origin,
in the nucleusmakes ATP using oxygenits own small genomemakes ATP without oxygenlittle or no DNAproteinsmakes no ATP at alla remnant
WHERE IT STARTSA mitochondrionThe organelle most eukaryotic cells have. It carries out aerobic cellular respiration, and it still has a small genome of its own, with many more of its genes in the nucleus.
ALTERED · IN MANY EUKARYOTES THAT LACK MITOCHONDRIAA hydrogenosomeA small organelle that generates ATP by anaerobic processes, without oxygen. It has little or no DNA.The giveaway is in the nucleus: genes of mitochondrial origin, coding for proteins that work inside the hydrogenosome. So hydrogenosomes appear to be highly altered mitochondria, adapted to life where oxygen is scarce.1
REDUCED FURTHER · IN OTHER ANAEROBIC EUKARYOTESA mitosomeA still smaller organelle that also appears to be a remnant mitochondrion. It has lost all capacity for metabolism, so it makes no ATP.It does retain the genes needed to assemble the clusters of iron and sulfur found in many proteins. Why those genes in particular are kept remains unknown.

A sketch. The sources say hydrogenosomes are small and mitosomes smaller still, and give no measurements.

THE CLOSEST RELATIVES OF THE HOST

The Asgard archaea

an archaeon: no nucleusarm-like projections, function unknown
2015The genome of an archaeon from hot springs on the floor of the Arctic Ocean was pieced together. It turned out to be a close relative of eukaryotic cells, with genes like those that organize the inside of a eukaryotic cell.1
SINCE THENSimilar archaea were soon found in many environments around the world, and are now grouped as the Asgard archaea. By 2021 more than 600 kinds had been identified, and one had been grown in the laboratory.

INFOGRAPHIC 30
INTERACTIVE · TWO HYPOTHESES FOR THE ORIGIN OF THE EUKARYOTIC CELL

Which came first: the nucleus, or the symbiosis?

Tap a button to explore
HYPOTHESIS 1 · NUCLEUS FIRSTarchaeonnucleus formsengulfs iteukaryoteHYPOTHESIS 2 · SYMBIOSIS FIRSTarchaeonmoves innucleus formseukaryote
HYPOTHESIS 1The host was already a true eukaryoteIn this view the archaeal ancestor had already changed enormously before it met the bacterium. It had a nucleus, a cytoskeleton and an internal membrane system, but only a limited ability to get energy out of organic molecules.Then it engulfed a proteobacterium capable of aerobic respiration, which became the mitochondrion.The difficulty: no one has ever found a eukaryote that does not have, and never had, mitochondria.1
HYPOTHESIS 2There was no eukaryotic cell before mitochondriaIn this view the eukaryotic cell as a whole began as a symbiosis between an archaeon and a proteobacterium.The proteobacterium became the mitochondrion and gave many genes to the nuclear genome. The archaeon gave others, including the genes for transcribing DNA and translating it into proteins. The nucleus came afterwards.
TAP A HYPOTHESISSame ingredients, same result, different orderBoth hypotheses start with an archaeon and a proteobacterium and end with a eukaryote that has mitochondria. They disagree about which came first: the nucleus, or the symbiosis.
WHAT BOTH EXPLAINWhy the eukaryotic genome is a hybrid, with some genes like those of bacteria and others like those of archaea.
WHAT NEITHER FULLY EXPLAINSThe origin of the nucleus, of linear chromosomes, of the eukaryotic cytoskeleton, or of a cytoplasm divided up by membranes.

5 · Trophic cascades
INFOGRAPHIC 36
INTERACTIVE · ANIMATION · THE WOLVES OF YELLOWSTONE, IN SIX STAGES

From wolves to a river: the story of a cascade

Tap the buttons, or Next stage, to click through all 6
no wolves: elk graze the valley barewolves return: elk leave the valleywillow and aspen grow backsongbirds and beavers move inbeaver ponds: ducks, fish and moreroots hold the banks: the river steadies
STAGE 1 · WITHOUT THE TOP PREDATORElk eat the valley downWith no wolves, elk and deer graze wherever they like, including along the rivers. Young willow and aspen are eaten before they can grow. The banks are bare.
STAGE 2 · TOP DOWNThe wolves change how the elk behaveWolves kill some elk. Just as important, the elk change their behavior: they stay out of the valleys and gorges where they are easy to catch.This is a top-down effect. It starts at the top of the food web and works its way down.
STAGE 3 · ONE LEVEL FURTHER DOWNThe plants regenerateWhere the elk no longer browse, willow and aspen grow back and the trees grow tall. Primary production goes up in exactly the places the elk now avoid.Wolves never touch a tree. This is an indirect effect.
STAGE 4 · OTHER SPECIES FOLLOWSongbirds and beavers move inMore trees means nesting places and food, so songbirds return. More willow means food and building material for beavers, and beavers build dams.
STAGE 5 · AN ENGINEER TAKES OVERThe cascade keeps spreadingBeavers are the classic ecosystem engineer: a dam turns a stream into a pond, and a pond is a home for ducks, fish and other animals.The effects keep branching. This is why it is said that wolves give life to many others.
STAGE 6 · EVEN THE PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHYThe story ends at the river itselfRegenerating forest stabilizes the banks. Roots hold the soil, so there is less erosion, and the river settles into a steadier channel.As the story is told, a predator changed the behavior of its prey, which changed the plants, which changed the shape of the land. This last link is the hardest to show, and how much of it is down to wolves is debated.

This is the story as it is usually told, and it shows what a trophic cascade means. In the real park other things matter as well, and how large the wolf effect is remains debated.

8 · Trophic efficiency: where the energy goes
INFOGRAPHIC 40
INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW 1,000 UNITS OF ENERGY

Three filters between a plant and a herbivore

Tap the buttons, or Next filter, to click through all 4
plants made
1,000eaten

500DETRITUSDETRITUSDETRITUSassimilated

START · WHAT THE PLANTS MADE1,000 units of energy in plant tissueThis is the net primary production: the energy stored in the plants that a herbivore could, in principle, eat. Follow it to see how much becomes herbivore.
FILTER 1 · CONSUMPTION EFFICIENCYNot everything gets eatenConsumption efficiency (CE) is the fraction of production at one trophic level that is consumed by the next. Here the herbivores eat 500 of the 1,000: CE = 500 ÷ 1,000 = 50%.The rest is never eaten. It dies and becomes detritus.
FILTER 2 · ASSIMILATION EFFICIENCYNot everything eaten is digestedAssimilation efficiency (AE) is the fraction of the food consumed that is assimilated. A lot of what is eaten cannot be digested and leaves as feces.Here 250 of the 500 is assimilated: AE = 250 ÷ 500 = 50%.
FILTER 3 · PRODUCTION EFFICIENCYMost of what is digested gets burnedProduction efficiency (PE) is the fraction of the assimilated food that is turned into new consumer biomass. Most of it is used to make ATP and power the body, and leaves as heat.Here 100 of the 250 becomes new tissue: PE = 100 ÷ 250 = 40%.Trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE = 0.50 × 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.10. That is the 10%.

A worked example with round numbers that land on the 10% average. Real values differ from one ecosystem to another.

INFOGRAPHIC 41
DIAGRAM · DIGESTION IS HARD WORK

Why production efficiency is so low

has not eaten recentlyhas just eatenheartgut hard at work

A python that has just eaten is working far harder than one that has not: its heart and gut are running at full tilt just to deal with the meal. All of that work is paid for with energy from the food, and it leaves as heat. Only what is left over can become new snake.

Endosymbiosis & Food Webs

Where mitochondria and chloroplasts came from, and how energy and effects travel through a food web.

02 / 30 · PART 1 · THE QUESTION

Endosymbiosis

The mitochondria powering your cells were once free-living bacteria. How do we know?

03 / 30 · PART 1 · 1 OF 13

A bacterial cell: what it has and what it lacks

The theory is about bacteria that ended up living inside other cells. So start with the bacterium itself. Unlike a eukaryotic cell, a bacterial cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts, and most of its DNA is a single circular chromosome.1,2

INTERACTIVE · ONE BACTERIAL CELL, THREE VIEWS

Look inside a bacterium

Tap the buttons, or Next view, to click through all 3
cell wallcell membraneflagellumribosomescytoplasmplasmidone circular chromosomeno nucleusno mitochondriano chloroplastsproteins in the membraneproteins in the cytoplasm
WHAT A BACTERIAL CELL HASSmall and simple, but a complete living thing
A CELL MEMBRANE AND A CELL WALLThe membrane encloses the cell. The wall sits outside it and holds the cell's shape.
ONE CIRCULAR CHROMOSOMEMost of the cell's DNA is a single circular molecule, folded into many loops. It sits loose in the cytoplasm, with nothing around it.
RIBOSOMES IN THE CYTOPLASMThey build the cell's proteins. With no nucleus in the way, they sit right beside the DNA.
SOMETIMESPlasmids: small extra circles of DNA. Flagella: tails that let some bacteria swim.
WHAT A BACTERIAL CELL LACKSNo nucleus, no mitochondria, no chloroplastsThe dashed shapes are the three things a bacterial cell does not have.The DNA is still there, faint in the middle. It simply has no membrane around it, so there is no nucleus.Hold on to this. The whole theory is about how eukaryotic cells came to have two of these three.
WHERE THE ENERGY WORK HAPPENSOn the membrane and in the cytoplasmA bacterium has no mitochondria, yet it still has to get energy out of food. That work is done by proteins floating in the cytoplasm or embedded in the cell membrane.A few bacteria, notably the photosynthetic ones, also have internal membranes, and their light reactions happen there.In a eukaryotic cell the same two jobs happen inside organelles: aerobic respiration in the mitochondrion, photosynthesis in the chloroplast.

A simplified drawing. Prokaryotic cells are small: typically 1 to 2 micrometers across, much smaller than eukaryotic cells.1

04 / 30 · PART 1 · 2 OF 13

Binary fission

When bacterial cells divide, they do it by binary fission: the cell copies its DNA, grows, and splits in two. Eukaryotic cells divide by different processes, mitosis and meiosis.1,2

INTERACTIVE · SIX FRAMES

Watch one cell become two

Tap the buttons, or Next step, to click through all 6
attached to the membraneone circle of DNAcopying starts at one spotand runs both ways roundtwo attachment sitestwo circles of DNAthe sites move apartthe cell gets longerpinches in at the middleabout twice its first sizetwo daughter cellssame DNA in each
1 · BEFORE DIVIDINGOne circular DNA molecule, attached to the membraneThe cell's circular chromosome is held against the inside of the cell membrane by proteins (the pink dot).
2 · COPY THE DNAReplication starts at one spot and runs both waysBinary fission begins with DNA replication. Copying starts at a specific location, the origin of replication, and proceeds in opposite directions around the circle.
3 · TWO CIRCLESEach copy gets its own attachment siteThe result is two DNA molecules, each attached to the membrane at a different site. At first the two sites are close together.
4 · GROWThe cell lengthens and the copies move apartAs the cell elongates, the two attachment sites are carried away from each other, and each takes its DNA circle with it.
5 · PINCHA constriction forms at the midpointWhen the cell is about twice its original size and the two DNA molecules are well separated, the cell pinches in at the middle.
6 · TWO CELLSNew membrane and wall finish the jobNew cell membrane and cell wall are built at the constriction, dividing the one cell into two.Each daughter cell has the same genetic material as the parent cell.
05 / 30 · PART 1 · 3 OF 13

Two free-living bacteria, and the cell that engulfed them

Before any of this happened there were no mitochondria and no chloroplasts anywhere. There were bacteria living on their own, and there was a larger cell that could swallow things. Meet the two bacteria first, as they were: free.1,2

THE FIRST BACTERIUM

An alpha-proteobacterium

Bacterium · free-living
FREE-LIVING: no cell around itdividing on its ownoxygen + food in
WHAT IT ISA member of the proteobacteria, the most diverse of all the groups of bacteria. The alpha-proteobacteria are one branch of that group.1,2
HOW IT LIVESOn its own. It takes in small organic molecules and oxygen from its surroundings and gets its energy by aerobic respiration.
INSIDENo nucleus, one circular chromosome. It is a typical bacterial cell, like the one in Step 1.
ITS PART IN THE STORYIts descendants become the mitochondrion.
06 / 30 · PART 1 · 4 OF 13

Two events on the tree of life

Endosymbiosis has been fundamentally important to the origin of eukaryotes. Now that you have met the cells, see where the story sits on the tree of life: two separate events, each one a line of bacteria joining a line of eukaryotes and staying.2

INTERACTIVE · THE TREE OF LIFE, AND TWO LINEAGES THAT MOVED IN

Where mitochondria and chloroplasts came from

Tap a button to explore
rootBACTERIAEUKARYOTESalpha-proteobacteriacyanobacteriaother bacteriaARCHAEAother eukaryotesplants + other
photosynthesizersanimalsfungi
THE TREE OF LIFEThree domains, and one of them is oursEvery living thing belongs to one of three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukaryotes. Read the tree from the root to the tips: time runs that way, and every tip is alive today.Animals and plants are twigs on a single branch, the eukaryotes (boxed). Mitochondria and chloroplasts are found only on that branch.
EVENT 1 · GAVE RISE TO MITOCHONDRIAA line of bacteria joins the stem of the eukaryotesFollow the amber line. It leaves the alpha-proteobacteria branch and meets the eukaryote stem at the flashing dot. That meeting is the engulfing, about 2 billion years ago.2The dot sits on the stem before the point where today's eukaryote groups split apart. So the amber line then runs up every one of those branches: all eukaryotes inherited mitochondria.
EVENT 2 · GAVE RISE TO CHLOROPLASTSA second line of bacteria joins one eukaryote branchFollow the green line. It leaves the cyanobacteria branch and meets just one eukaryote branch, the one leading to plants and other photosynthetic eukaryotes.It joins after the split, so only that branch carries it. Animals and fungi are on other branches and never had chloroplasts. The cell it joined already carried the amber line, so mitochondria came first.
WHAT THE LINES MEANNothing jumped. A lineage moved in and has been inherited ever sinceA bacterium did not turn into a eukaryote, and it did not hop from one domain to another. One bacterium was taken inside a host cell and kept dividing there. Each time the host cell divided, its daughter cells received some of them. That has continued, without a break, to this day.So every mitochondrion in you is a direct descendant of that one engulfed bacterium. The two white rings mark the common ancestors: from there, one line stayed free-living and leads to today's bacteria, and the other went inside and leads to today's organelles. They are relatives.Each event belongs to a branch, at one point along it. Everything that descends from that point inherited the organelle. Event 1 sits below the branching point of the living eukaryotes, Event 2 above it.
TAP THE FOUR BUTTONS IN ORDERWhere on the tree did the two organelles come from?The amber and green lines are lines of descent, like every other branch on the tree. Watch where each one comes from, where it joins, and where it goes afterwards.

A simplified tree. Only the branches that matter for this story are named, and branch lengths mean nothing.

07 / 30 · PART 1 · 5 OF 13

One cell living inside another

Symbiosis is a close interaction between species that has evolved over a long time. Endosymbiosis is a symbiosis in which one species lives inside the other.1,2

THE THEORY OF ENDOSYMBIOSIS Mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria. They were engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells and became a permanent part of them.

Lynn Margulis championed this theory. Endosymbiosis has been fundamentally important to the origin of eukaryotes.

ancestral
eukaryotic cellfree-living
bacteriumone cell, the bacterium
living on inside it
08 / 30 · PART 1 · 6 OF 13

Two engulfing events, in order

The host did not start out with mitochondria or chloroplasts. It gained them one at a time, by engulfing a bacterium and keeping it.2

EVENT 1 · ABOUT 2 BILLION YEARS AGO

The alpha-proteobacterium moves in

1The host, an ancestral eukaryotic cell with no mitochondria, meets a free-living alpha-proteobacterium.
2The host engulfs it, most likely as prey: a predator swallowing its food.
3It is not digested. It survives inside the host.
4Over a very long time it becomes the mitochondrion.
09 / 30 · PART 1 · 7 OF 13

From those two events to you and to plants

Follow the host cell forward. One branch of its descendants stopped after Event 1. Another went through Event 2 as well.2

STRAIGHT OUT OF EVENT 2

Red algae, green algae, and then land plants

common ancestorafter Event 2red algaegreen algaeland plants

The engulfing of a cyanobacterium happened in a common ancestor of the green algae and the red algae. Both groups inherited its chloroplasts. Land plants arose later, from among the green algae, and carry the same chloroplasts.1

Their chloroplasts are wrapped in two membranes, which is what an engulfed cyanobacterium would leave behind.

10 / 30 · PART 1 · 8 OF 13

What to notice in each one

Both still carry clear signs of where they came from: their own DNA and more than one membrane.2

MITOCHONDRION

The cell's power supply

outer membraneinner membrane, foldedits own circular DNA
WHAT IT DOESCellular respiration. It makes most of the ATP that powers cellular functions.
WHERE IT CAME FROMA free-living alpha-proteobacterium.
WHAT TO NOTICETwo membranes, its own circular DNA, and it divides by binary fission.

Testing the theory: five predictions

Nobody watched any of this happen. So the theory is tested the way any claim about the past is tested: if it is true, what should we still be able to see today?2

Eukaryotes with no mitochondria

Most eukaryotic cells contain mitochondria, but a few single-celled eukaryotes that live in oxygen-free environments do not. Does that break the rule that all eukaryotes have them? Biologists had two ways to explain these cells.1

THE FIRST HYPOTHESISThey branched off before mitochondria existedBiologists originally thought these eukaryotes were leftovers from a time before Event 1: cells with a nucleus that had never taken in the bacterium.That proposal was abandoned. These cells turned out to have genes in their nucleus that migrated there from the mitochondrial symbiont. A cell that never had the symbiont could not have its genes.
THE SUPPORTED HYPOTHESISThey had mitochondria once, and lost themThe textbook reports that every mitochondria-free eukaryote examined has relict mitochondrial genes in its nuclear genome (the amber dots).1So their ancestors went through Event 1 like every other eukaryote. These organisms live in oxygen-free environments, and over time their mitochondria were lost or, as the next drawing shows, altered to suit life without oxygen.
14 / 30 · PART 1 · 12 OF 13

Still open: the origin of the eukaryotic cell itself

If mitochondria began as proteobacteria and chloroplasts as cyanobacteria, where did the rest of the eukaryotic cell come from? This is where settled science ends and active research begins.1

from the bacterial symbionts from other bacteria found only in eukaryotes related to archaea

Where this part comes from

The small numbers in the text point to this list.

16 / 30 · PART 1 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in

  1. A bacterial cell has no nucleus, no mitochondria and no chloroplasts. Most of its DNA is one circular chromosome, and it divides by binary fission.
  2. Mitochondria descended from free-living alpha-proteobacteria. Chloroplasts descended from free-living cyanobacteria. Each was engulfed by an ancestral eukaryotic cell and became an obligate mutualist living inside it: an endosymbiont.
  3. Mitochondria came first. The cyanobacterium was engulfed by a cell that already had mitochondria.
  4. Nothing jumped between domains. The engulfed bacteria kept dividing inside their hosts and have been inherited ever since.
  5. Mitochondria do cellular respiration. Chloroplasts do photosynthesis. A plant cell has both organelles, so it does both.
  6. Five lines of evidence: size, circular DNA, binary fission, two or more membranes, and DNA sequences.
  7. The conclusive one is the DNA sequences: the organelles' DNA nests inside those bacterial groups.
  8. Thousands of genes became dozens. Some moved to the nucleus, and others were lost because they were not needed inside a cell.
  9. A few eukaryotes have no mitochondria. They lost them, and still carry mitochondrial genes in the nucleus, so mitochondria remain a universal feature of all eukaryotes: every eukaryote descends from a cell that had them.
  10. How and when the nucleus first originated is not resolved. It is still an active area of research.

Food webs

Some organisms make their own food and the rest get theirs from other organisms. So who eats whom, and what happens to everyone else when one species disappears?

Two ways to get food

Part 1 ended with two kinds of eukaryotic cell: one with chloroplasts and one without. Among eukaryotes, that difference goes with two ways of getting food.

HAS CHLOROPLASTSIt can make its own foodPlants and algae photosynthesize with their chloroplasts. Cyanobacteria, the bacteria chloroplasts came from, were photosynthesizing long before and still do. All of these are autotrophs.

Direct and indirect effects

Because everything in a web is connected, a change in one species reaches others it never touches.

DIAGRAM · EFFECTS, NOT ENERGY

Foxes help grass without ever touching it

Arctic foxesGeeseLemmingsGrasses−−−−+
Direct effect Indirect effect

These arrows show who affects whom, so they are not food web arrows. Foxes eat geese and lemmings. Geese and lemmings eat grass. More foxes means fewer grazers, which means more grass.

22 / 30 · PART 2 · 5 OF 11

Trophic cascades

When a top predator influences the density of species at every trophic level below it, that is a trophic cascade. It is a chain of indirect effects that starts at the top.

INTERACTIVE · ANIMATION · THE WOLVES OF YELLOWSTONE, IN SIX STAGES

From wolves to a river: the story of a cascade

Tap the buttons, or Next stage, to click through all 6
no wolves: elk graze the valley barewolves return: elk leave the valleywillow and aspen grow backsongbirds and beavers move inbeaver ponds: ducks, fish and moreroots hold the banks: the river steadies
STAGE 1 · WITHOUT THE TOP PREDATORElk eat the valley downWith no wolves, elk and deer graze wherever they like, including along the rivers. Young willow and aspen are eaten before they can grow. The banks are bare.
STAGE 2 · TOP DOWNThe wolves change how the elk behaveWolves kill some elk. Just as important, the elk change their behavior: they stay out of the valleys and gorges where they are easy to catch.This is a top-down effect. It starts at the top of the food web and works its way down.
STAGE 3 · ONE LEVEL FURTHER DOWNThe plants regenerateWhere the elk no longer browse, willow and aspen grow back and the trees grow tall. Primary production goes up in exactly the places the elk now avoid.Wolves never touch a tree. This is an indirect effect.
STAGE 4 · OTHER SPECIES FOLLOWSongbirds and beavers move inMore trees means nesting places and food, so songbirds return. More willow means food and building material for beavers, and beavers build dams.
STAGE 5 · AN ENGINEER TAKES OVERThe cascade keeps spreadingBeavers are the classic ecosystem engineer: a dam turns a stream into a pond, and a pond is a home for ducks, fish and other animals.The effects keep branching. This is why it is said that wolves give life to many others.
STAGE 6 · EVEN THE PHYSICAL GEOGRAPHYThe story ends at the river itselfRegenerating forest stabilizes the banks. Roots hold the soil, so there is less erosion, and the river settles into a steadier channel.As the story is told, a predator changed the behavior of its prey, which changed the plants, which changed the shape of the land. This last link is the hardest to show, and how much of it is down to wolves is debated.

This is the story as it is usually told, and it shows what a trophic cascade means. In the real park other things matter as well, and how large the wolf effect is remains debated.

25 / 30 · PART 2 · 8 OF 11

Trophic efficiency: where the energy goes

Trophic efficiency is the amount of energy at one trophic level divided by the amount at the level below it. It is small because, at three separate points, energy fails to reach the next level.

INTERACTIVE · FOLLOW 1,000 UNITS OF ENERGY

Three filters between a plant and a herbivore

Tap the buttons, or Next filter, to click through all 4
plants made
1,000eaten
500eaten
500eaten
500not eaten
500not eaten
500not eaten
500DETRITUSDETRITUSDETRITUSassimilated
250assimilated
250feces 250feces 250new biomass
100respired 150
leaves as heat
START · WHAT THE PLANTS MADE1,000 units of energy in plant tissueThis is the net primary production: the energy stored in the plants that a herbivore could, in principle, eat. Follow it to see how much becomes herbivore.
FILTER 1 · CONSUMPTION EFFICIENCYNot everything gets eatenConsumption efficiency (CE) is the fraction of production at one trophic level that is consumed by the next. Here the herbivores eat 500 of the 1,000: CE = 500 ÷ 1,000 = 50%.The rest is never eaten. It dies and becomes detritus.
FILTER 2 · ASSIMILATION EFFICIENCYNot everything eaten is digestedAssimilation efficiency (AE) is the fraction of the food consumed that is assimilated. A lot of what is eaten cannot be digested and leaves as feces.Here 250 of the 500 is assimilated: AE = 250 ÷ 500 = 50%.
FILTER 3 · PRODUCTION EFFICIENCYMost of what is digested gets burnedProduction efficiency (PE) is the fraction of the assimilated food that is turned into new consumer biomass. Most of it is used to make ATP and power the body, and leaves as heat.Here 100 of the 250 becomes new tissue: PE = 100 ÷ 250 = 40%.Trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE = 0.50 × 0.50 × 0.40 = 0.10. That is the 10%.

A worked example with round numbers that land on the 10% average. Real values differ from one ecosystem to another.

↑ TOTAL IMPACT OF THE SPECIES
KEYSTONEsmall biomass, big impactDOMINANTbig biomass, big impactmost species

A dominant species matters because there is so much of it. A keystone species matters far more than its amount would suggest. An ecosystem engineer is defined differently: by what it does to the habitat.

29 / 30 · PART 2 · LOCK IT IN

Lock it in

  1. Autotrophs make their own food. Heterotrophs get it from other organisms. Photo- means light, chemo- means chemical.
  2. Food web arrows point from the food to the eater, the direction the energy moves.
  3. Count the levels below an organism to name it. One that eats from two or more levels is a trophic omnivore.
  4. Direct effects are between species that interact. Indirect effects pass through a species in between.
  5. A trophic cascade starts with a top predator and reaches every level below, flipping direction each time.
  6. A pyramid of energy is always widest at the base. About 10% of the energy at one level reaches the next.
  7. Trophic efficiency = CE × AE × PE: the fraction eaten, times the fraction assimilated, times the fraction turned into new biomass.
  8. Keystone: impact out of proportion to its biomass. Dominant: big impact because there is so much of it. Engineer: it changes the habitat.
  9. Parasites and decomposers are left off most food webs, but a disease that removes a keystone species reshapes the whole community.

Quiz

50 questions: 24 on endosymbiosis, 22 on food webs, and 4 on the energy terms from the same reading. Pick an answer to see whether it is right and why.

QUESTION 1 OF 50Mitochondria descended from…

Correct. Not quite. Mitochondria were once free-living alpha-proteobacteria.

QUESTION 2 OF 50Chloroplasts descended from…

Correct. Not quite. Chloroplasts were once free-living cyanobacteria, which are photosynthetic bacteria.

QUESTION 3 OF 50Which came first?

Correct. Not quite. The cyanobacterium was engulfed by a eukaryotic cell that already had mitochondria. All eukaryotes have mitochondria, but only some have chloroplasts.

QUESTION 4 OF 50Which line of evidence is the most convincing?

Correct. Not quite. Molecular phylogenies place mitochondrial DNA within the alpha-proteobacteria and chloroplast DNA within the cyanobacteria.

QUESTION 5 OF 50How do mitochondria and chloroplasts divide?

Correct. Not quite. Binary fission is how bacteria divide. Eukaryotic cells use mitosis and meiosis.

QUESTION 6 OF 50A mitochondrion has its own DNA, and so does a chloroplast. In both of them, that DNA is organized as…

Correct. Not quite. Both are circular. A mitochondrion and a chloroplast each carry their own genome as a circular DNA molecule, just as alpha-proteobacteria and cyanobacteria do.

QUESTION 7 OF 50Having two or more membranes is consistent with…

Correct. Not quite. More than one membrane is what you would expect of a cell that was taken inside another cell.

QUESTION 8 OF 50Free-living bacteria have thousands of genes. Why do mitochondria and chloroplasts have only dozens?

Correct. Not quite. Inside a host cell, many genes were no longer needed, and some migrated to the nucleus.

QUESTION 9 OF 50What is the main job of a mitochondrion?

Correct. Not quite. Mitochondria carry out cellular respiration, which makes the ATP that powers cellular functions. Chloroplasts do photosynthesis. A mitochondrion does carry its own DNA, but that is a clue to its origin, not its job.

QUESTION 10 OF 50A few eukaryotes have no mitochondria. Why are mitochondria still called a universal feature of eukaryotes?

Correct. Not quite. Their ancestors had mitochondria. The leftover genes in the nuclear genome show it.

QUESTION 11 OF 50Endosymbiosis means…

Correct. Not quite. Endo means inside. Symbiosis is a close, long-evolved interaction.

QUESTION 12 OF 50Over time, the engulfed bacterium and its host became…

Correct. Not quite. Both benefited, and eventually neither could do without the other.

QUESTION 13 OF 50Auto- in autotroph means…

Correct. Not quite. Auto- means self and hetero- means other. Photo- means light and chemo- means chemical.

QUESTION 14 OF 50In a food web, an arrow runs from grass to elk. What does it show?

Correct. Not quite. Arrows go from the organism being eaten to the organism eating it, the direction the energy moves.

QUESTION 15 OF 50An organism eats only primary producers. It is a…

Correct. Not quite. There is exactly one trophic level below it.

QUESTION 16 OF 50In ecology, a trophic omnivore is an organism that…

Correct. Not quite. A consumer that eats both primary and secondary consumers is a trophic omnivore even if it never eats a plant.

QUESTION 17 OF 50In the Yellowstone web, wolves eat elk and beaver, and also berries. Wolves are best described as…

Correct. Not quite. Elk and beaver are primary consumers and berries are producers, so wolves feed on two trophic levels.

QUESTION 18 OF 50Which group is often left out of food web drawings?

Correct. Not quite. Decomposers feed on the dead remains of every level, yet they are often missing from the drawing.

QUESTION 19 OF 50Arctic foxes eat geese. Geese eat grass. The effect of foxes on grass is…

Correct. Not quite. Foxes never touch the grass. By lowering the geese, they leave more grass.

QUESTION 20 OF 50Elk and moose both eat willows, and neither eats the other. The effect of elk on moose is…

Correct. Not quite. It travels through the willows they both eat.

QUESTION 21 OF 50A trophic cascade starts with a change in…

Correct. Not quite. Then it reaches every trophic level below, flipping direction at each one.

QUESTION 22 OF 50Wolves return to Yellowstone and elk decline. What should happen to willows and aspen?

Correct. Not quite. Fewer elk, and warier elk, means less browsing.

QUESTION 23 OF 50A keystone species is one that…

Correct. Not quite. The seastar Pisaster is the classic example.

QUESTION 24 OF 50Maple trees are very common in many eastern North American forests and shape those forests as a result. Maples are…

Correct. Not quite. Their impact is large because there is so much of them.

QUESTION 25 OF 50Why are beavers ecosystem engineers when wolves are not?

Correct. Not quite. Wolves reshape the community through who they eat, not by rebuilding the habitat.

QUESTION 26 OF 50When seastars were removed from a stretch of rocky shore, the number of species…

Correct. Not quite. The seastar kept space open by eating mussels. Without it, mussels crowded out most other species.

QUESTION 27 OF 50Why does trophic omnivory make it hard to predict what happens when a consumer is removed from a food web?

Correct. Not quite. Omnivory is common, and it increases the number of indirect effects running through the web.

QUESTION 28 OF 50A disease kills most of the seastars on a rocky shore. Based on the removal experiment, what should happen?

Correct. Not quite. Losing the seastars to disease has the same effect as removing them by hand. Parasites and disease can reshape a food web through their hosts.

QUESTION 29 OF 50In a pyramid of energy, where is the amount of energy highest?

Correct. Not quite. The base is much larger than the level above it, and each level above is smaller again.

QUESTION 30 OF 50On average, about how much of the energy in one trophic level is transferred to the next?

Correct. Not quite. About 10%. That is the rule of thumb to use when you are not given the three efficiencies.

QUESTION 31 OF 50Consumption efficiency is 50%, assimilation efficiency is 50% and production efficiency is 40%. What is the trophic efficiency?

Correct. Not quite. Trophic efficiency is the product of the three: 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.10, which is 10%.

QUESTION 32 OF 50Primary producers hold 10,000 units of energy. You are given no efficiencies. About how much production should there be in the primary consumers?

Correct. Not quite. With no efficiencies given, use the rule of thumb: about 10% moves up. 10% of 10,000 is 1,000.

QUESTION 33 OF 50On the tree of life, the organelles of eukaryotes arose from which domain?

Correct. Not quite. Both events start on the bacterial branch: an alpha-proteobacterium gave rise to mitochondria and a cyanobacterium gave rise to chloroplasts.

QUESTION 34 OF 50Which statement about photosynthetic eukaryotes is true?

Correct. Not quite. Chloroplasts are found in all photosynthetic eukaryotes. Diatoms, brown algae, dinoflagellates and many other algae photosynthesize and are not plants. They all have mitochondria too.

QUESTION 35 OF 50In a food chain drawn Grass → Elk → Wolf, what does each arrow show?

Correct. Not quite. Arrows point from the food to the eater, because that is the direction the energy moves.

QUESTION 36 OF 50A tree shrew feeds on a pitcher plant's nectar and leaves its droppings in the pitcher, which gives the plant nitrogen. What kind of interaction is this?

Correct. Not quite. Both gain: the shrew gets food and the plant gets nitrogen. The plant is still a primary producer.

QUESTION 37 OF 50A python that has just eaten has its heart and gut working at full tilt. What does this show about energy?

Correct. Not quite. It is why production efficiency is low: only what is left over after the work of living can become growth.

QUESTION 38 OF 50Livestock use most of the world's farmland but supply a much smaller share of our food calories. Why?

Correct. Not quite. An extra trophic level is expensive: only about 10% of the energy is passed on.

QUESTION 39 OF 50Sea star wasting syndrome kills seastars along a coast. Based on the seastar removal experiment, what should happen next?

Correct. Not quite. A disease that removes a keystone species has the same effect as removing it by hand.

QUESTION 40 OF 50Which players are usually missing from a food web drawing even though they matter?

Correct. Not quite. Food webs are usually drawn without them, but both can change a community as much as a predator can.

QUESTION 41 OF 50What does binary fission start with?

Correct. Not quite. The circular chromosome is copied first. Each copy is attached to the membrane, and the sites move apart as the cell grows.

QUESTION 42 OF 50Is a cyanobacterium a chloroplast?

Correct. Not quite. Free-living cyanobacteria are still alive today. That is what lets us compare them with chloroplasts.

QUESTION 43 OF 50Event 2, the engulfing of a cyanobacterium, happened in the common ancestor of which groups?

Correct. Not quite. Land plants arose later from among the green algae, so they carry the same chloroplasts.

QUESTION 44 OF 50Did a bacterium jump into the eukaryote domain?

Correct. Not quite. Its free-living relatives are still bacteria today. The organelles are relatives of those bacteria, inherited inside eukaryotic cells.

QUESTION 45 OF 50A chloroplast has 60 to 200 genes. Its closest free-living relatives have 2,000 to 3,000. Where did the rest go?

Correct. Not quite. Genes moved when chloroplasts broke open, and on viruses. Many still make proteins that go back into the chloroplast.

QUESTION 46 OF 50A hydrogenosome is best described as:

Correct. Not quite. It has little or no DNA, but the cell's nucleus carries genes of mitochondrial origin that make its proteins. A mitosome is reduced further and makes no ATP.

QUESTION 47 OF 50What do the Asgard archaea suggest?

Correct. Not quite. They have genes like those that organize a eukaryotic cell. Mitochondria still came from an alpha-proteobacterium.

QUESTION 48 OF 50In the standard picture, where does a mitochondrion's outer membrane come from?

Correct. Not quite. The bacterium's own membrane becomes the inner one. The real history is more complicated, so remember the number: two or more.

QUESTION 49 OF 50Paulinella chromatophora matters because:

Correct. Not quite. It shows endosymbiosis is not a one-time accident, and that the change from bacterium to organelle can still be in progress.

QUESTION 50 OF 50When the DNA of a chloroplast's small ribosomal RNA gene is compared:

Correct. Not quite. Like a bacterium and unlike the cell it lives in: the organelle came in from outside.
